posts.text:
A little good news. And some reasons to keep going. 🌍

Three things have particularly struck me this week.

1. Progress often comes from consistency rather than spectacular innovation.

The World Health Organization reports that 63 countries have now eliminated at least one neglected tropical disease, up from 42 in 2020. The number of people requiring interventions has fallen by 36% since 2010.

This is the result of sustained work: medicines, vaccination, sanitation, surveillance and healthcare reaching communities that have historically been overlooked.

It isn’t glamorous. It is life-changing.

2. Nature can recover when we give it the opportunity.

A family of six beavers has been released into the Loch Ness catchment in Scotland, around 500 years after they were last recorded there.

Beavers are ecosystem engineers. They create wetlands, support biodiversity, improve water quality and can help reduce flooding.

A small family of animals, with potentially enormous consequences for the surrounding landscape.

3. Some of the most important discoveries happen because somebody notices what others have overlooked.

On Indonesia’s Bangka Island, a tiny primate, the Bangka slow loris, once feared possibly extinct, has been documented by local rescuers.

Their records have identified more than 90 individuals, with 86 rehabilitated and released into the wild.

A reminder that conservation isn’t always led by large international organisations. Sometimes it begins with local people who refuse to look away.

And there is more worth celebrating:

🧠 Stanford researchers have identified brain activity patterns that may help predict Alzheimer’s vulnerability years before symptoms emerge. Early research, but potentially significant for future prevention.

👁️ Researchers are growing miniature human eye lenses from stem cells, creating new opportunities to study cataracts and test treatments.

These developments won’t solve everything. The funding gaps in global health remain serious, biodiversity is still under enormous pressure, and none of these scientific findings is an instant cure.

But perhaps that is precisely the point.

The world is not only shaped by the people making the most noise. It is also shaped by scientists, healthcare workers, conservationists, volunteers and ordinary people quietly doing difficult, important work.

We shouldn’t ignore the things going wrong.

But we shouldn’t overlook the things going right, either.

People are still showing up. And quite a lot of them are doing extraordinary things, often without much recognition at all.

I think that’s worth remembering.

🚀 ANTICIPATING RISKS & BUILDING RESILIENT HR IN THE AGE OF AI & DISRUPTION 2027

Entering 2027, HR must move beyond administrative duties to become a Strategic Architecture and Value Creator that protects EBITDA margins and long-term business sustainability.

Key insights from the Impactful Leadership Team Research (Nov 2026) and the HR Director’s Manifesto:

🔥 5 Key HR Risk Mitigation Matrices & KPIs for 2027:

🟢 1. AI Ethics & Data Privacy Risk

📌 Impact: 3–5% EBITDA drop from privacy fines, litigation, and employer brand damage.

📌 Strategy: Form an AI Ethics Committee, apply Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) frameworks, and audit algorithms bi-annually.

📌 KPI: 100% AI ethics audit compliance; 0 data leaks.

🔵 2. Loss of Future Talent Pipelines

📌 Impact: Up to 45% recruitment cost inflation and long-term productivity loss.

📌 Strategy: Launch an AI-Augmented Apprenticeship Framework and redesign entry-level roles into AI Operators/Supervisors.

📌 KPI: >85% junior talent retention; 40% internal manager promotions.

🟡 3. Legal & Regulatory Compliance (Indonesia)

📌 Impact: Termination wage back-pay, labor dispute fines, and forced conversion of PKWT to permanent status.

📌 Strategy: Comprehensive contract audits, outsourcing restructuring, and proportional SUSU updates.

📌 KPI: 0 lost PHI court cases; 100% compliant contracts.

🔴 4. Managerial Burnout Risk
📌 Impact: 25% managerial turnover, poor operational decisions, and stalled strategy execution.

📌 Strategy: Implement a Managerial Detox Framework using Multi-Agent Systems to automate 40% of admin tasks.
📌 KPI: >95% middle manager retention; +35% coaching time.

🟣 5. Skill Obsolescence Risk

📌 Impact: Productivity decline and consultant dependency costs up to 12% of total payroll.

📌 Strategy: Transition to a Skills-Based Organization with real-time automated skill inventories and an Internal Talent Marketplace.

📌 KPI: >70% organizational skill fit index; 50% internal talent mobility.

💡 
"Administrative HR manages the present cost; Strategic Architecture engineers the future return on capital. As long as the CHRO speaks the language of activity rather than capital efficiency, HR will remain a line item on the expense sheet—never a driver of market valuation." — Joko Agus H., Author of The CEO’s Compass & HR Director’s Manifesto

🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS FOR EXECUTIVES:

Proactively manage risks for business continuity

Treat talent as a strategic capital asset
Deploy AI with ethical, human-centric governance

Position HR as a future driver of enterprise valuation

📲 Ready to protect your EBITDA margins in the AI era?

FROM ALMATY TO JAKARTA: Bringing Formula One's High-Performance Leadership Lessons to Indonesia.

What can Formula One teach us about building better businesses, leading stronger organisations and winning through uncertainty? I found some fascinating answers in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

At CREW Central Asia 2026 URBAN FUTURE 2026, I had the privilege of meeting and sharing the stage with Xevi Pujolar, an accomplished Formula One engineer and executive whose career spans more than two decades across five F1 teams, including Jaguar, Williams, HRT, Toro Rosso and Sauber.

Having worked alongside exceptional drivers, including Fernando Alonso and Max Verstappen, Xevi brings a wealth of firsthand experience from one of the world's most demanding competitive environments.

What particularly impressed me was how he translated the realities of Formula One into practical lessons for business and leadership.

His message was powerful: Trust. Preparation. Resilient systems. Continuous reinvention.

A two-second pit stop may look like an extraordinary display of individual skill. In reality, it represents years of preparation, disciplined teamwork, precise communication and a system designed to perform under pressure.

I believe these lessons have enormous relevance for Indonesia. As our country enters another important chapter of economic development, attracting investment and creating opportunities will require more than ambition.

This is why I see tremendous value in bringing international expertise and real-world experience into Indonesia's business community. My next ambition is to bring this conversation from Almaty to Jakarta.

I would love to see Xevi Pujolar share his extraordinary Formula One experience with Indonesian entrepreneurs, investors, corporate executives, business owners and the next generation of leaders through a dedicated high-performance leadership forum.

Imagine translating lessons from the Formula One pit wall into better decision-making, stronger management, more resilient organisations and a new mindset for Indonesian businesses.

I am grateful to Xevi for the inspiring exchange in Almaty. Sometimes, one conversation opens the door to an opportunity that deserves to reach a much wider audience.

Read my full article on Indonesia Rising: https://lnkd.in/gtbzm6S5

Are you a business organisation, corporate leader, institution or event organiser interested in bringing this conversation to Jakarta? We would welcome the opportunity to explore a collaboration.

RL (Rusmin Lawin)

posts.text:
. Area Pekerjaan di Foto Ini
Yang terlihat di foto adalah Drill Floor & Derrick Area di sebuah Jack-up Rig / Drilling Rig offshore.

Ini adalah jantungnya operasi pengeboran:
• Derrick / Menara Bor: Struktur baja tinggi di tengah foto. Tempat pipa bor (drill pipe) disusun vertikal sebelum dimasukkan ke dalam sumur. 
• Drill Floor: Lantai kerja utama tempat tim pengeboran beroperasi. Di foto, area yang diterangi lampu sorot dengan railing kuning. • Pipe Rack / Catwalk: Jalur di kiri bawah tempat pipa-pipa bor diletakkan horizontal sebelum diangkat ke drill floor. 
• Deck Bawah: Area untuk kontainer kargo, peralatan pendukung, genset, dan jalur evakuasi. 
Di area ini, operasi berjalan 24 jam non-stop, dibagi 2 shift 12 jam.
2. Safety di Area Ini
Ini termasuk Red Zone / High-Risk Area. Aturannya sangat ketat:
• PPE Wajib: Helm, kacamata safety, sarung tangan, coverall tahan api (FRC), sepatu safety, ear protection, dan H2S detector personal. 
• Permit to Work & Toolbox Meeting: Tidak ada pekerjaan yang dimulai tanpa izin kerja dan briefing risiko sebelum shift
. • Handrail & Fall Protection: Semua railing kuning yang terlihat itu wajib. Bekerja di ketinggian di derrick harus pakai full body harness dan lanyard.
 • Lifting Safety: Area di bawah beban yang diangkat crane / hoist adalah zona terlarang. Harus selalu waspada terhadap dropped object. • Housekeeping: Deck harus bersih dari oli dan sisa material agar tidak licin, apalagi di tengah laut yang berangin.
 • Emergency Ready: Jalur evakuasi, muster point, lifeboat, dan alat pemadam harus selalu bisa diakses, seperti yang terlihat di sisi kanan foto. 
Prinsipnya: Stop Work Authority. Siapapun boleh menghentikan pekerjaan jika melihat kondisi tidak aman.
3. Peralatan yang Terlihat di Foto 
• Top Drive / Travelling Block: Alat gantung kuning besar di tengah derrick, berfungsi memutar dan mengangkat rangkaian pipa bor.
 • Drill Pipe: Tumpukan pipa hitam vertikal di dalam derrick.
 • Drawworks / Hoisting System: Mesin pengangkat utama untuk naik-turun pipa. • BOP (Blow Out Preventer): Terletak di bawah drill floor, untuk mencegah semburan liar (kick/blowout) dari sumur. 
• Mud System & Shale Shaker: Untuk sirkulasi lumpur bor dan memisahkan cutting. 
• Crane & Cargo Container: Kontainer biru di kanan untuk logistik material. 
• Floodlight & Genset: Lampu sorot untuk penerangan operasi malam hari.  
4. Siapa yang Bekerja di Sini? • Drilling Crew: Driller, Assistant Driller, Derrickman (yang kerja di atas derrick), Floorman / Roustabout (yang kerja di drill floor).
 • Toolpusher / Rig Superintendent: Pimpinan tertinggi di rig, penanggung jawab operasi dan safety.
 • HSE Officer: Mengawasi kepatuhan safety dan izin kerja.
 • Mechanic, Electrician, & Welder: Tim maintenance untuk semua mesin dan kelistrikan.
 • Mud Engineer, Directional Driller, Company Man: Perwakilan dari operator / klien yang mengawasi jalannya pengeboran. • Marine Crew & Radio Operator: Mengatur stabilitas rig, cuaca, dan komunikasi dengan darat. 
• Catering & Housekeeping: Mendukung kehidupan sehari-hari kru di atas rig.

Indonesia punya berapa banyak engineer: ratusan ribu atau jutaan? 🤔⚙️

Sebelum membandingkan angka, ada satu pertanyaan yang perlu dijawab: siapa yang sedang dihitung?

Sarjana teknik, praktisi insinyur, hingga pemegang sertifikasi dan registrasi memiliki cakupan yang berbeda. Definisi, sumber, dan tahun data perlu diperhatikan agar kesimpulannya tepat. 📊

Bagi Teknikers yang sedang membangun karier, angka tersebut bisa menjadi awal untuk melihat lebih jauh: bidang apa yang dibutuhkan, kompetensi apa yang dicari, dan pengalaman apa yang perlu dipersiapkan?

Mulai dari langkah yang konkret: perkuat dasar engineering, pahami dokumen teknis, kuasai software beserta asumsi dan batasannya, lalu bangun portofolio yang bisa dijelaskan dan dipertanggungjawabkan. 🛠️

Geser sampai slide terakhir untuk melihat kaitannya dengan pengembangan karier Teknikers! 👉

💬 Teknikers berasal dari disiplin apa, dan kompetensi apa yang sedang dikembangkan? Ceritakan di kolom komentar!

📌 Simpan sebagai pengingat belajar dan bagikan ke rekan Teknikers lainnya.

𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗮 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗺𝗶 𝗝𝗮𝗱𝗶 𝗥𝗮𝗷𝗮 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝘂 𝗕𝗮𝗿𝗮 𝗗𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗮! 𝗧𝗮𝗽𝗶, 𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗽𝗸𝗮𝗵 𝗸𝗶𝘁𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝗸𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗻𝘆𝗮? 🏗️

Berdasarkan data terbaru, Indonesia berhasil menduduki posisi puncak sebagai pemasok batu bara termal terbesar di dunia dengan volume mencapai 240,3 juta ton, meninggalkan Rusia yang mengalami penurunan ekspor. Sebuah pencapaian luar biasa bagi sektor energi kita! 📈

Namun, di balik target produksi yang masif ini, ada tanggung jawab besar yang tidak bisa diabaikan. Menjadi "Raja" bukan sekadar soal volume, melainkan 𝙎𝙊𝘼𝙇 𝙎𝙏𝘼𝘽𝙄𝙇𝙄𝙏𝘼𝙎.

Produksi tinggi berarti penggalian yang lebih dalam dan timbunan (waste dump) yang jauh lebih besar. Di sinilah peran krusial Rekayasa Geoteknik dibutuhkan. Kesalahan analisis bisa berakibat fatal—mulai dari ancaman keselamatan hingga penghentian operasi yang merugikan miliaran rupiah. 🚨

Untuk menjawab tantangan ini, Akademi Tambang Indonesia mempersembahkan:
🎓 𝐂𝐄𝐑𝐓𝐈𝐅𝐈𝐄𝐃 𝐄𝐗𝐂𝐋𝐔𝐒𝐈𝐕𝐄 𝐖𝐎𝐑𝐊𝐒𝐇𝐎𝐏: 𝐏𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐤𝐚𝐲𝐚𝐬𝐚 𝐆𝐞𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐤𝐧𝐢𝐤 𝐝𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐦 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐦𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐚𝐧(𝐀𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐋𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐠 𝐓𝐚𝐦𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐠, 𝐄𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐬𝐢 𝐖𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞 𝐃𝐮𝐦𝐩, 𝐝𝐚𝐧 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐚𝐧 𝐆𝐞𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐤𝐧𝐢𝐤)

My Journey with AWS AI Academy and Dicoding Indonesia!

I'm excited to share that I have successfully completed the AWS AI Academy 2026 training program conducted by Dicoding Indonesia and earned my certificate.
Throughout this learning journey, I explored a comprehensive curriculum that covered Spec-Driven Development dengan Kiro, foundational cloud concepts and generative AI implementations in Belajar Dasar Cloud dan Gen AI di AWS, fundamental programming concepts through Memulai Pemrograman dengan Python, as well as core machine learning concepts via Belajar Machine Learning untuk Pemula. The hands-on modules and structured curriculum provided immense clarity on how modern intelligent systems are architected and deployed.
In particular, the experience helped me understand how to leverage scalable cloud infrastructure to build, train, and deploy models efficiently, effectively bridging the gap between theoretical machine learning concepts and actual end-to-end industry solutions. Beyond the technical skills, the program encouraged a structured approach to problem-solving and inspired me to continuously explore cutting-edge tools within the AI ecosystem.
As I continue my journey in Computer Science and Software Development, I believe that every new skill, challenge, and learning experience brings me one step closer to becoming a better engineer.
A huge thank you to AWS AI Academy and Dicoding Indonesia for delivering such an impactful learning experience and supporting developers in expanding their technical horizons! 💻✨

Dalam riset komprehensif terbaru kami:

- 4 Pilar Arsitektur Enterprise: Hybrid reasoning core, grounded vector memory, sandboxed tool calling, dan tata kelola kedaulatan data sesuai UU Perlindungan Data Pribadi (UU PDP No. 27/2022).
- Studi Kasus Riil Distributor B2B: Waktu penyelesaian order dipangkas dari 42 menit menjadi 18 detik instan dengan payback period 5,4 bulan.

Perangkat lunak cerdas bukan dinilai dari kepandaiannya bersilat lidah, melainkan dari presisinya dalam mengeksekusi proses bisnis yang menghasilkan laba nyata.

🚀 SUPPLY CHAIN DIGITALIZATION: JANGAN ASAL BELI SOFTWARE!

Banyak perusahaan merasa sudah melakukan digital transformation karena punya ERP, WMS, TMS, Power BI, sampai AI. Tapi pertanyaannya: apakah semua sistem itu benar-benar terintegrasi dan menghasilkan keputusan bisnis yang lebih baik?

Dalam Supply Chain Management, ada 4 kelompok teknologi yang perlu dipahami:

📊 1. ANALYTICS TOOLS
Excel, Power BI, Tableau.
Mengubah data menjadi insight untuk monitoring KPI, inventory turnover, OTIF, biaya distribusi dan profitability.

📦 2. INVENTORY TOOLS
Cin7, Zoho Inventory, inFlow, Katana.
Mengontrol stock availability, replenishment, purchasing, inventory accuracy dan production tracking.

📈 3. PLANNING TOOLS
SAP IBP, Kinaxis, o9, OMP, RELEX.
Mendukung demand forecasting, S&OP, supply planning, inventory optimization dan scenario simulation.

🔗 4. CONNECTED PLATFORMS
Oracle SCM, Microsoft Dynamics 365, Blue Yonder, Manhattan, Infor, Coupa.
Menghubungkan procurement, warehouse, transportation, supplier hingga customer.

🇮🇩 INSIGHT UNTUK INDONESIA

Menurut saya, tantangan terbesar perusahaan Indonesia bukan kekurangan software, tetapi fragmented data dan lemahnya integrasi antarproses.

Bayangkan:

- Sales menggunakan Excel sendiri.
- Warehouse menggunakan WMS yang tidak terhubung dengan ERP.
- Transport menggunakan aplikasi GPS berbeda.
- Purchasing punya database supplier sendiri.
- Management baru mendapatkan laporan beberapa hari kemudian.

Akibatnya, perusahaan punya banyak data, tetapi belum tentu punya visibility!

Menariknya, studi GS1 US yang dirilis 3 November 2026 menemukan hampir 60% organisasi sudah menggunakan advanced automation atau AI, tetapi hanya 38% yang memiliki integrasi data terpusat secara real-time.

MY TAKE:

Sebelum investasi software jutaan bahkan miliaran rupiah, pastikan 5 hal:

1. Master data SKU, customer dan supplier harus konsisten.
2. Tentukan single source of truth.
3. Integrasikan ERP, WMS, TMS dan planning system.
4. Tetapkan KPI dan data ownership yang jelas.
5. Siapkan training, change management dan kompetensi SDM.

Untuk Indonesia, integrasi ini semakin penting karena distribusi melibatkan banyak pulau, multi-warehouse, distributor, principal dan transport partner.

Remember: Digital Transformation is not about how many software you own, but how well your systems work together!

posts.text:
Masa depan industri konstruksi Indonesia tidak lagi sekadar tentang siapa yang bisa membangun paling cepat atau paling murah, tapi siapa yang mampu mengelola DATA secara akurat di sepanjang siklus hidup bangunan. 🏗️📊

Pemikiran inilah yang menjadi fondasi tim kami saat menyusun strategi tender Pembangunan Gedung Asrama Putri A5 IPB di ajang The 13th ICEF, IPB University. Kami menolak untuk hanya mempresentasikan gambar visual. Sebaliknya, kami mendemonstrasikan eksekusi integrasi BIM 3D hingga 7D secara komprehensif.

Mengapa sampai 7D? Karena sebuah bangunan bukan hanya soal fase konstruksi, tapi investasi puluhan tahun ke depan. Berikut breakdown workflow yang kami kembangkan (geser slide untuk detail dokumentasinya):

🔹 3D (Modeling & Coordination): Menggunakan Autodesk Revit untuk memodelkan struktur dan arsitektur dengan tingkat presisi tinggi sejak fase pradesain, memastikan perhitungan elemen seperti penulangan dan floor-to-floor akurat.

🔹 4D (Scheduling): Menyusun penjadwalan proyek menggunakan Microsoft Project, lalu mengintegrasikannya ke dalam Autodesk Navisworks untuk menyimulasikan visualisasi urutan kerja konstruksi. Hal ini memudahkan kami mengidentifikasi potensi clash jadwal dan bottleneck di lapangan.

🔹 5D (Costing): Melakukan ekstraksi Quantity Take-Off (QTO) dan Rebar Schedule secara otomatis. Transparansi data ini krusial untuk menekan overbudget dan meminimalisir human error dalam perhitungan RAB.

🔹 6D (Sustainability): Menggunakan software Tally, kami menyusun Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) untuk menganalisis jejak karbon (Global Warming Potential) dan potensi energi tak terbarukan dari material. Pendekatan ini kami selaraskan dengan target Netral Karbon dan tujuan pembangunan berkelanjutan (SDGs), memastikan asrama tidak hanya kuat, tapi ramah lingkungan.

🔹 7D (Facility Management): Mengelola Common Data Environment (CDE) melalui Trimble Connect. Kami merancang basis data digital untuk memudahkan manajemen pemeliharaan aset (maintenance), pelacakan status elemen, dan kolaborasi tim di masa depan.

Lewat workflow ini, kami membuktikan bahwa integrasi teknologi adalah kunci untuk mengontrol anggaran secara transparan dan menjamin keberlanjutan pasca-konstruksi. Alhamdulillah kami sangat bersyukur visi besar ini membuahkan hasil Juara 2 Nasional bersama rekan satu tim yang luar biasa: Mutiaradinda Haidar, Oscar Abdullah Husain, dan Reivalda Aulia Anggraeni Nugraha. 🏆🚀

Pengalaman ini menjadi pembuktian bagi kami bahwa integrasi data yang menyeluruh adalah langkah pasti menuju industri konstruksi yang lebih presisi, efisien, dan berkelanjutan di masa depan.

1. APA ITU SPP-TDLN?
SPP-TDLN adalah Sistem Pemungutan Pajak atas Transaksi Digital Luar Negeri. Sistem ini dibentuk untuk memperluas mekanisme pemungutan PPN atas pemanfaatan barang dan jasa digital dari luar negeri di Indonesia.
Dasar hukumnya adalah:
●      Peraturan Presiden Nomor 68 Tahun 2025
●      PMK Nomor 49 Tahun 2026
SPP-TDLN bukan jenis pajak baru dan tidak mengubah tarif PPN. Sistem ini melengkapi mekanisme PPN PMSE, khususnya untuk transaksi yang belum dipungut PPN melalui mekanisme tersebut.

2. MENGAPA BANK DAN FINTECH DILIBATKAN?
Pemerintah melibatkan bank dan lembaga fintech tertentu sebagai penerbit atau issuer. Pada tahap awal, terdapat enam issuer, yaitu BRI, Bank Mandiri, BNI, BTN, BSI, dan Link Aja. Melalui sistem yang terintegrasi, informasi transaksi pembayaran digunakan untuk mengidentifikasi transaksi digital luar negeri yang memenuhi kriteria pengenaan PPN. Artinya, infrastruktur pembayaran kini menjadi bagian dari infrastruktur administrasi perpajakan.

3. APAKAH TRANSFER ANTAR BANK IKUT DIKENAKAN PPN?
Tidak. Transfer antar bank, pemindahan dana pribadi, maupun transfer melalui dompet digital tidak otomatis dikenakan PPN melalui SPP-TDLN.
Objek pemungutannya adalah pemanfaatan barang dan jasa digital dari luar negeri yang memenuhi ketentuan perpajakan. 

4. APA DAMPAKNYA BAGI PERUSAHAAN?
Perusahaan saat ini banyak menggunakan layanan digital asing, seperti:
●      Software dan aplikasi berlangganan
●      Cloud computing dan data storage
●      Digital advertising
●      Platform teknologi dan layanan digital lainnya
Beberapa hal yang perlu dilakukan:
●Inventarisasi seluruh langganan layanan digital luar negeri
●Cek apakah penyedia sudah memungut PPN 
●Identifikasi transaksi yang berpotensi masuk cakupan SPP-TDLN
●Pastikan bukti pembayaran dan dokumen perpajakan tersimpan dengan baik
●Evaluasi pencatatan biaya serta perlakuan PPN Masukan sesuai ketentuan
Jangan sampai perusahaan membayar layanan digital setiap bulan, tetapi tidak memahami implikasi administrasi dan perpajakannya.

PESAN KARSA ADVISORY
Perubahan sistem perpajakan tidak selalu ditandai dengan munculnya tarif atau jenis pajak baru. Terkadang, perubahan paling signifikan justru terjadi pada infrastruktur pemungutannya. SPP-TDLN menunjukkan bahwa pemerintah semakin mengintegrasikan sistem pembayaran dengan administrasi perpajakan. Bagi dunia usaha, ini bukan sekadar isu pajak digital. Ini adalah pengingat bahwa transaksi bisnis semakin transparan, terintegrasi, dan semakin mudah ditelusuri.
 
Pajak Bukan Sekadar Kepatuhan. Pajak adalah Bagian dari Strategi Bisnis.

posts.text:
On this day, 49 years ago, a YF-16 fired two AIM-7F Sparrow missiles at China Lake in California at approximately 18,000 feet and Mach 0.9 and 1.05 in the first all-weather Sparrow launches from the F-16, following the type's first Sparrow firing on October 6. General Dynamics was demonstrating an all-weather, radar-guided capability that could appeal to foreign customers, although the USAF had not required it for its own production F-16s.

That distinction carried into the production F-16A/B, whose APG-66 radar could detect and track airborne targets but lacked the continuous-wave illumination needed to employ the Sparrow's semi-active radar seeker. Unlike the infrared-guided AIM-9 Sidewinder, the AIM-7F could engage targets beyond visual range and in poor visibility, but its seeker depended on radar energy reflected from the target. The firing aircraft had to maintain radar illumination throughout the missile's flight, keeping the target within its radar's tracking and illumination envelope until intercept.

The limitation eventually drove the Air Defense Fighter (ADF) conversion, which modified the APG-66 and added a dedicated continuous-wave (CW) illuminator to the radar antenna assembly, alongside other radar and software changes. The resulting F-16A/B ADFs entered the Air National Guard interceptor role in 1989, getting their first AIM-7 target-drone kill on February 23. F-16C/Ds equipped with the APG-68 could employ the Sparrow through the radar's high-PRF pulse-Doppler illumination capability, with an F-16C completing its first Sparrow firing on May 2, 1989.

General Dynamics also pursued integration with existing export customers, proposing ADF-like modifications for early F-16A/Bs operated by Egypt, Pakistan, Venezuela, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, while at the time, Greece and Turkey showed interest in adapting their APG-68-equipped F-16C/Ds.

U.S. Air National Guard, Bahrain and Taiwan fielded the AIM-7 Sparrow on their F-16s before moving onto the AIM-120 AMRAAM, while Iraq received AIM-7M-F1/H missiles for its F-16IQs. Egypt has also continued relying on the Sparrow as the U.S. has repeatedly withheld AMRAAM approval for its F-16 fleet over sensitivities with Israel.

posts.text:
I’m fed up with how difficult cross-border payments are in Bangladesh.

Building a global software business here sometimes feels like having overprotective parents. Well-meaning, but so afraid of something going wrong that every step needs permission. Eventually, the child never gets the freedom or confidence to grow independently.

Look at India, Malaysia and Indonesia. They’re finding ways to connect businesses to global payment infrastructure while maintaining regulatory oversight.

If we expect the worst from every company just because some bad actors exist, our good actors will never get the opportunity to bring clean foreign currency into the country, create value and strengthen Bangladesh’s position in the global economy.

What I’m asking for is simple:

* Transparent, risk-based access to international payment gateways.
* Easier foreign currency accounts and cross-border settlements for legitimate tech exporters.
* Regulation that targets bad actors without punishing everyone else.

We’re not asking for reckless freedom. We’re asking for trust, because trust builds confidence, and confidence builds businesses.

Dear Government, Please Let us grow here, earn globally and contribute to Bangladesh instead of being pushed to incorporate elsewhere just to get paid.

📌 Low-Latency FPGA Multi-Tap Echo Architecture with Atomic Zero-Crossing Runtime Updates
🗓 Tue, Nov 10 · 17:00–18:30 (ICT) · Courtyard 4

📌 Hardware-Software Co-Design of a Heterogeneous Neuromorphic SoC for Time-Series Signal Processing
🗓 Wed, Nov 11 · 08:30–10:00 (ICT) · Courtyard 4
Special Session: Hardware Accelerators for AI-Driven and Real-Time Signal Processing Systems (HAAI)

Both works focus on FPGA-based hardware for real-time signal processing, from RTL architecture to on-board validation on the Kria KV260. The first is a spatial echo processor that updates its parameters only at zero crossings, removing zipper noise without smoothing filters. The second fuses DWT and FFT preprocessing with a time-multiplexed spiking neural network that scales to 32,768 virtual neurons.

If you're attending APSIPA ASC 2026, feel free to drop by either session or reach out. I'd love to connect and talk about digital hardware design, signal processing, and hardware accelerators.

posts.text:
Indonesia's central government still has about Rp990 trillion to spend in November and December. For anyone selling software to it, the tighter limit is the calendar.

Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara gave the figure after a November 3 meeting with President Prabowo, who asked ministries to keep year-end spending efficient (ifakta, Disway).

The Treasury's year-end rules, PER-9/PB/2026, set the dates:
1. A contract has to be registered with the local treasury office (KPPN) within 5 working days of signing.
2. Contractual payment orders are accepted only until December 23.
3. Work handed over on December 19–23 is paid through RPATA, a year-end holding account.

The budget year closes on December 31. That's awkward for SaaS, because a 12-month subscription signed in December runs into 2027. Under Perpres 46/2025, a contract that spans more than one budget year needs prior approval from the authorized official.

A practical step: plan a Q4 public-sector proposal backwards from December 23.
1. Is the purchase already in this year's budget (DIPA) and procurement plan (RUP)?
2. Can the first order end on December 31, with 2027 bought as a separate order?
3. Who signs the handover document (BAST), and on what date?

A deal that misses those dates usually waits for the next budget cycle.

If you sell to government, which year-end date catches deals out most often?

#GovTech #B2BSales #Indonesia

72 hours. 4 distinct engineering paradigms. 1 unified national bioethanol infrastructure

At the Greenovate Challenge 2026 Hackathon  (organized by Global Greenchem Innovation & Network Programme Indonesia , Universitas Pertamina, UNIDO, and Yale University), I competed alongside 62 top selected innovators from across Indonesia and be The First Winner.

Over 3 days and 2 nights, I led our team to build:"A GIS-Powered Network of Multi-Feedstock, Multi-Line Bioethanol Biorefineries for Indonesia's E5/E10 Transition."
My core focus as team lead was turning four deep-tech specialties into one unified system:
1. Geospatial Scouting (GIS): Mapped multi-feedstock biomass potential across regions by Novandra Fiqriansyah
2. Process Efficiency (Aspen Plus): Optimized multi-line biorefinery conversion and yields.
3. Circular Logistics & HIP Pricing: Minimized supply chain costs and calculated an optimal Bioethanol Market Index Price (HIP) 
4. Full-Stack Integration: Connected every spatial, thermodynamic, and pricing model into a single, real-time upstream-to-downstream monitoring dashboard by Edward Worang


The takeaway: Combining and maximizing the peak potential of every specialized domain is non-negotiable. You cannot build sustainable, agile, and relevant national policy in isolation—it requires engineering, economics, and software working as one.

⚡ 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗶𝗹 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆-𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘀?

Could yesterday's producing wells help store tomorrow's electricity?

Research is exploring 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗱-𝗮𝗶𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 (𝗖𝗔𝗘𝗦) in petroleum infrastructure, sometimes coupled with geothermal heat.

🔹 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀—𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗲.

In CAES, surplus electricity powers compressors. Pressurized air is stored, then withdrawn and expanded to generate electricity.

• 𝗪𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲: an isolated, sealed wellbore acts as a pressure vessel. Capacity is limited by usable well volume and pressure rating.
• 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲: air occupies pore space in permeable rock, fracture space, or both. Capacity and deliverability depend on reservoir properties, gas–water displacement, and containment.

Oldenburg & Pan (2013) and Wang & Bauer (2017) modeled porous-formation CAES. Wang et al. (2025) assessed a depleted sandstone gas field in Australia; their proposed 600 MW, 12-hour scheme still faced deliverability limitations in simulation.

Hu et al. (2025) modeled how cycling and wettability affect pore-scale air–water displacement and working-gas availability. Bi et al. (2026) instead modeled storage in hydraulic-fracture space. Young et al. (2021) explored fractured shale using compressed natural gas—not air.

🔹 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝘁?

Air warms on compression and cools on expansion. Rock–gas heat exchange can affect pressure, energy recovery, and cycling performance.

Zhang et al. (2025) modeled geothermal heating of air inside sealed wells: reported round-trip efficiency rose from 52.21% to 61.75% (9.54 percentage points). Yang et al. (2026) explored transient behavior under assumed formation temperatures.

Other designs differ. Bai et al. (2026) evaluated geothermal-assisted CAES assuming an idealized depleted-gas reservoir, while Wu & Su (2026) integrated CAES with a geothermal-driven organic Rankine cycle, plus modeled hydrogen and water production.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱—not field-proven. Comparisons must account for external geothermal heat and differing system boundaries.

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱.

Is there sufficient working-gas capacity and deliverability? Can casing, cement, seals, and faults tolerate repeated pressure–temperature cycles? Could oxygen react with residual hydrocarbons? Will heat recharge sustainably—and will reuse be viable?

A retired or plugged well is not automatically a reusable storage asset.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮: The subsurface may support not just energy extraction, but energy storage. Moving from simulation to deployment requires integrated geology, reservoir engineering, geomechanics, well integrity, and energy-system analysis.

#EnergyStorage #GeothermalEnergy #SubsurfaceEngineering #EnergyTransition

posts.text:
I just launched Velora Suites, a hotel and short-let website I designed and built from scratch. 

It started as a simple idea: a booking site that feels as premium as the stay itself. It ended up as a full system with two sides.

For guests:
* Room pages with image carousels
* Facilities, restaurant menu, and a filterable gallery with a lightbox
* A booking request form and a contact form
* A layout that works properly on phones, tablets, and desktops

For the hotel team:
* A secure admin dashboard with live stats
* Full control to add, edit, and delete rooms, facilities, and gallery photos (with image uploads)
* Review booking requests and manage statuses (pending, confirmed, or cancelled) 
* Read messages directly from guests

Tech Stack: PHP, MySQL, HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript.

The part that taught me the most was making it feel right on a phone. Fixing the mobile menu, the hero section, the carousel swiping, and the admin tables took more iterations than the initial build... but it was absolutely worth it.

🔗 Check it out live here: https://lnkd.in/eVbvxFrk

I'd love your honest feedback, especially on the mobile experience!

And if any business owners in my network need a premium website like this, my inbox is open. I am also actively looking for web development roles, so if you know of any teams hiring, let's connect.

posts.text:
AI can write the code.
A good software engineer still has to know whether it should ship.
I use AI every day as a frontend developer.
It helps me learn faster and improve the way I work.
The judgment about what reaches production still stays with me.
𝟭. 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿?
Subscriptions, API usage, infrastructure, maintenance, and review time belong in the same calculation as hiring.
The leverage is real.
A lower total cost still has to be proven.
𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲?
When I ship incorrect code, my team investigates and owns the fix.
When AI generates that code and I merge it, responsibility stays with:
• The person who reviewed it
• The team that released it
• The company that set the process
The provider supplies the tool.
Shipping remains a human decision.
𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲?
Over the next five years, companies will look for engineers who can frame a problem, choose an architecture, review generated code, protect security, and maintain what they ship.
𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜 𝗮𝗺 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴
• Fundamentals: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and the browser
• Problem framing and architecture
• Code review, debugging, and testing
• Security and product judgment
• Clear communication with design, product, and engineering
I plan to keep building these skills, use AI to learn faster, and understand every generated change before it reaches users.
I would like to hear your thoughts in the comments.
I respect your time, and I value every comment.

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
1. Has AI reduced your overall cost of software development?
2. Who should be accountable when AI-generated code causes a production issue?
3. Which skills are you focusing on to stay valuable over the next five years?

💬 𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. 😊 
There is a lot we can learn from each other. 👏

posts.text:
When Should a Business Hire a Freelance Developer, an IT Contractor, or a Development Agency?

Technology plays an important role in how modern businesses operate. From building websites and online stores to developing custom software and automating business processes, companies often need external technical expertise to bring their ideas to life.

But who should they hire? A freelance developer, an IT contractor, or a development agency?

Although these options can offer similar services, they differ in expertise, project management, availability, and working arrangements. Choosing the right one depends on the project's complexity, budget, timeline, and long-term requirements.

1. Hiring a Freelance Developer

A freelance developer is an independent professional who works directly with clients on specific projects or technical tasks. Common specializations include WordPress, frontend and backend development, eCommerce, mobile applications, and website maintenance.
For example, a small business that needs a WordPress website, a payment gateway integration, or a few website improvements may not need an entire development team.

A freelancer is often suitable when:

•The project has a clearly defined scope.
•Only one or two technical skills are required.
•The business has a limited development budget.
•Direct communication with the developer is preferred.
•The client can manage project coordination.

The main advantage is flexibility and direct access to the person doing the work. However, one developer may not have expertise in every area a project requires. Availability can also become a concern when ongoing support or several tasks are needed simultaneously.

2. Working With an IT Contractor

An IT contractor is an independent specialist engaged for a specific period, assignment, or technical responsibility. Contractors often work alongside an existing business or internal technical team.

For example, a company may hire a contractor to integrate business software, manage technical infrastructure, support an existing development team, or implement a specialized system.

An IT contractor may be the right choice when:

•The business needs specialist expertise temporarily.
•An internal team requires additional technical support.
•A particular system needs implementation or maintenance.
•Hiring a permanent employee is not necessary.
•The project has defined technical responsibilities.

Contractors allow businesses to access specialized skills without making a long-term employment commitment. However, the business may still need to manage project planning, coordination, and other responsibilities internally.

3. Partnering With a Development Agency

A development agency provides technology services through a coordinated team. Depending on its structure, the team may include developers, designers, project managers, and quality assurance specialists.

This arrangement is useful when a project involves several connected areas.

For example, building a multi-vendor marketplace may require frontend and backend development, vendor dashboards, payment integration, product management, testing, and ongoing maintenance. Coordinating all these responsibilities through one individual can be challenging.

A development agency may be more suitable when:

•The project requires multiple technical skills.
•Design and development must work together.
•Several systems or integrations are involved.
•Project management and testing are important.
•Ongoing development and support are expected.

An agency can provide a more coordinated approach, but businesses should still review its previous work, understand who will handle the project, and clarify communication, pricing, and deliverables.

4. Comparing the Three Options

Freelancer: Typically works independently on individual projects or specific development tasks. They are often a good choice for businesses that need focused expertise, flexibility, and a more cost-effective solution. Project management is usually handled by the client.

IT Contractor: Usually provides specialized technical expertise for a defined period or assignment. Businesses hire contractors when they need additional technical support, specific skills, or temporary development resources. Responsibilities may be shared between the contractor and the client.

Development Agency: Offers a coordinated team with expertise across multiple areas, such as development, design, testing, and project management. Agencies are generally better suited for complex projects, larger development requirements, or businesses looking for ongoing technical support.

These are general differences, not strict rules. Some freelancers manage large projects, IT contractors work independently or alongside internal teams, and smaller agencies may operate with limited resources. Ultimately, the right choice depends on your project's complexity, budget, technical requirements, and the level of support you need.

5. Which Option Is Best for Different Projects?

Business websites: A freelancer may be sufficient for a standard company website. Custom functionality, advanced integrations, or complex user systems may require additional specialists.

eCommerce stores: A freelancer can often build a basic WooCommerce or Shopify store. More complex requirements, such as inventory synchronization, custom checkout, and multiple integrations, may need broader expertise.

Custom software: An IT contractor can support an existing development team, while an agency may be better suited to projects requiring planning, design, development, testing, and deployment.

Multi-vendor marketplaces: These platforms often require buyer and seller accounts, vendor dashboards, commission management, payment processing, and order management. Businesses should look for relevant marketplace development experience.

Ongoing maintenance: Freelancers and contractors can handle routine updates and technical support. Businesses with several platforms or regular development requirements may benefit from an ongoing agency relationship.

6. What Should Businesses Check Before Hiring?

Before selecting a provider, businesses should consider a few important questions:

1. Have they completed similar projects?
2. Do they understand the required technologies?
3. Who will manage communication and project coordination?
4. What exactly is included in the quotation?
5. How will additional requirements affect cost and deadlines?
6. Will the business retain access to its source code, domain, hosting, and accounts?
7. What testing and post-launch support are included?

It is also important to establish milestones, payment terms, deadlines, and ownership of deliverables in writing.

A lower initial quotation does not always mean a lower overall cost. Poor documentation, incomplete functionality, and unexpected maintenance can increase expenses later.

Conclusion
There is no universally correct choice between a freelance developer, an IT contractor, and a development agency.

Freelancers are often suitable for smaller, clearly defined projects. IT contractors provide specialized expertise for temporary or ongoing technical responsibilities. Development agencies are useful when projects require multiple skills, coordinated delivery, and broader technical support.

Businesses should evaluate their requirements, budget, project complexity, and long-term expectations before deciding.

posts.text:
HR folks: how many of your last 500 fresher applications did you actually read?
Yesterday, someone on a YC co-founder matching call laughed at my startup idea. I posted about it on Reddit, got 22K views and a lot of honest feedback.
When I asked what the most painful part of the job hunt is, one person answered:
“Getting a response back even when you directly match the role like 100%.”
Candidates who fit aren’t getting seen. Hiring teams are buried in Easy Apply. I think both sides have the same problem: too many applications, too little signal.
So I’m rebuilding around one question:
What if you only saw the freshers who had already done the work?
→ Candidates learn for free, from what real job posts ask for
→ For one role, they complete a real work task
→ Every candidate gets the same structured interview: same questions, same rubric, about the work they just submitted
→ You get a ranked shortlist, with a report showing what each person built and how they scored
📎 Attached: a sample of the report you’d receive (fictional candidate, real format).
Why this method? A large 2022 meta-analysis on hiring (Sackett et al.) ranked structured interviews as the strongest predictor of job performance, with work-sample tests also near the top, ahead of general aptitude tests.
I’m starting with one role: frontend or full-stack interns for startups.
Honest questions for anyone who hires:
Would you shortlist from a report like this?
What would you need to see before trusting the rank?
What’s the most painful part of fresher hiring for you right now?
Looking for 3–5 early partners. Share one intern role, and I’ll run it as an open challenge and send you everyone who completes it, ranked, with reports. It’s new, so it could bring 5 candidates or 50. Free, no contract.
Comment or DM me. Every reply gets a response.

Hiring developers has become exhausting.

I'm a developer myself, so I know what that time costs.

So I started Stejar. You tell me what role you need, and I send you people I've checked myself. Backend, frontend, full-stack, data.

You try them for 2 weeks, paid. If it doesn't work out, I find you someone else for free and you only pay for the work that got done.

If this sounds familiar, write me.

posts.text:
Did you know that chess has long been a battleground for programmers? I didn’t, and not knowing that ended up costing me a lot of time.

When we started building ChessEver, my cofounder decided we should use Flutter, which was not the most common framework among chess developers. There were two reasons: it would make it easier to build an app for both iOS and Android, and Lichess also had a Flutter app. We thought that meant chess tools for Flutter would continue to improve.

But we ran into a serious issue right away: who was going to build our frontend? My cofounders weren’t frontend developers, so we found someone through a hiring service.

He was a great developer, but there was one major problem: he knew how the pieces moved, but not much else about chess. That led to communication issues I hadn’t anticipated.

For example, it never occurred to me to explain that what programmers might call a move is technically a half-move in chess notation. We write 1. e4 e5, not 1. e4 2. e5.
It became clear that we needed someone who understood chess well. But how could we find that person?

I started reaching out to people who had chess apps on the market. Most had built them using other technologies. I finally found someone who could have helped, but he quoted a very high price to adapt an open-source package to our app. It felt like his way of saying he wasn’t interested.

So, I widened my search and started contacting anyone who had built a chess app. That’s when I kept running into something surprising: many of these people did not care about chess.

I couldn’t understand it. Why were so many people building chess apps if they didn’t care about the game?

Then my cofounder said, “Vasif, keep in mind that chess has been a battleground for programmers.” I did some research and realized that developers often build chess-related projects to demonstrate their skills or challenge themselves.

That changed the way I searched. Instead of looking only for someone who had built a chess app, I started looking for someone who loved chess and happened to be a programmer.

Once I did that, I found a great developer who not only helps bring my ideas to life but also comes up with ideas of his own.

AI has improved tremendously since we started, and now even I can build cool things with it. But if you’re building a chess product, finding someone who loves the game can still save you a lot of time and help

Role: Full-Stack Next.js / TypeScript Engineer (SaaS & AI Infrastructure)
Location: Remote (India)
Type: Full-time / Long-term Contract
Email: hr@avantisofttech.com

About the Role
We are looking for an experienced Full-Stack Next.js / TypeScript Engineer to own technical maintenance, production reliability, and feature evolution for Statemento, a high-performance financial AI platform that converts complex bank statements into structured spreadsheets (Excel, CSV, QuickBooks).

Our entire stack is built in a modern, unified TypeScript ecosystem—no context-switching between backend languages. You will work directly on serverless architecture, AI extraction pipelines, database integrity, and webhook-driven billing systems.

What You’ll Do
Maintain & Scale the Core App: Own full-stack development across our Next.js App Router, React Server/Client Components, and Node.js serverless runtimes.

Refine AI Extraction Pipelines: Maintain and optimize document parsing workflows using LLM APIs (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI) and local PDF text processors (unpdf), ensuring strict balance reconciliation and zero data leakage.

Database & Auth Operations: Manage PostgreSQL on Supabase, write and deploy schema migrations, enforce strict Row-Level Security (RLS) policies, and debug connection pooling.

Payment & Subscription Lifecycle: Maintain our Merchant of Record integrations (Lemon Squeezy), including webhook event listeners, signature validation, idempotency guards, and customer entitlement syncs.

Production Reliability & Bug Triage: Monitor application health across Vercel, Supabase, and Upstash Redis. Diagnose and resolve edge-case PDF conversion issues and balance check discrepancies.

Testing & Code Quality: Run and expand automated test suites using TypeScript and Node’s native test runner (tsx).

What We’re Looking For
3–6 years of professional software engineering experience, with substantial production experience in TypeScript and modern Next.js (App Router).

Strong Database Fundamentals: Hands-on experience with PostgreSQL, schema design, and Supabase (specifically writing secure RLS policies).

Serverless & Webhook Proficiency: Solid understanding of stateless API design, HMAC signature verification, idempotency patterns, and asynchronous error boundaries.

Low-Level Data Handling: Comfortable working with Node.js streams, buffers (Uint8Array), and file transformations (CSV, XLSX).

Autonomous Problem Solver: High ownership mindset

Our Tech Stack
Frontend & Backend: Next.js (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
Data & Storage: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Upstash Redis (rate limiting)
Hosting & Runtime: Vercel Edge/Serverless, Node.js 24
AI & Document Processing: Anthropic Claude API, OpenAI API, unpdf, write-excel-file

I decided to fix that by building "Only Widget" — a high-performance, minimalist desktop widget for Windows & macOS that sits quietly on your desktop without choking system resources.
🚀 The Engineering Challenge:
Initially, the installer was ~118 MB and idle RAM hovered around 150 MB. For a simple widget, that was unacceptable. 
I re-architected the app from the ground up:
⚙️ Stack: Tauri 2.0 (Rust) + React 19 + Tailwind CSS
📊 Installer Size: Slashed from 118 MB down to 1.97 MB (98% reduction!)
🧠 Resource Usage: Drops to ~20-25 MB RAM with 0% CPU overhead
✨ Key Features:-- DOWNLOAD AND GIVE A TRY !!
• Real-time Network Telemetry: Live upstream & downstream bandwidth rates (Mbps / Kbps) refreshed every 1.5s
• 12-Hour Dual Digital Clocks: Local 12h AM/PM clock with synchronized world time zones (Sydney, London, NY)
• Native Desktop Pinning: Deep OS integration using Win32 API (HWND_BOTTOM) and macOS desktop level
• Modern Frosted Aesthetic: Glassmorphism border-glow, draggable, zero-clutter interface

Swipe to see the banner & a real screenshot of it running on my PC! 👇 📌 📌📌

💸 10 YOE ➔ 75 LPA

Senior Front-End Engineer - React & TypeScript Position Overview Build and enhance production web applications using modern React and TypeScript technologies. This role combines complex frontend engineering, scalable component design, state management, performance optimization, accessibility, and production troubleshooting. Youll work across application features, API integrations, testing, and UI architecture while collaborating with product, design, and QA to deliver maintainable, high-quality user experiences. What Youll Do / Key Responsibilities Build and maintain production web applications using React and TypeScript. Develop reusable components using React hooks, context, and component design patterns. Optimize application rendering, lazy loading, and frontend performance. Implement state management using Redux Toolkit and server-state libraries such as React Query. Build multi-step and conditional forms with schema-based validation. Integrate REST APIs and manage request lifecycles, caching, error handling, and request optimization. Develop component-based user interfaces using MUI, Emotion, and theming. Write automated tests using Jest, React Testing Library, and API mocking tools such as MSW. Implement accessible interfaces using semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support. Apply WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility practices. Monitor and optimize Core Web Vitals, bundle size, and code splitting. Use browser developer tools to profile and diagnose performance issues. Participate in Git workflows, merge requests, code reviews, and automated CI/CD quality gates. Debug production issues using logs, monitoring, and error-tracking tools. Communicate technical decisions, trade-offs, and implementation details effectively. Collaborate with product, design, and QA teams to deliver application features. Required Qualifications 5+ years building production web applications, with at least 3 years of React and TypeScript. Strong TypeScript and React experience, including hooks, context, component design, lazy loading, and avoiding unnecessary re-renders. Hands-on Redux Toolkit experience with selectors and a server-state library such as React Query, including caching, invalidation, and error handling. Experience building complex multi-step and conditional forms using react-hook-form or similar and schema-based validation such as yup or zod. Experience integrating REST APIs, managing request lifecycles and error states, and reducing unnecessary calls through techniques such as debouncing, batching, and optimistic updates. Experience with component frameworks such as MUI, CSS-in-JS such as Emotion, and theming. Testing experience with Jest and React Testing Library, mocking APIs with tools such as MSW, and writing tests that remain reliable through refactors. Practical accessibility experience with semantic HTML, keyboard and screen-reader

posts.text:
Years of experience is a lagging indicator. Scope is the signal.

I've been reading Indeed Hiring Lab's July report on seniority, and one methodology detail stuck with me more than the headline number.

The headline: in Q1 2026, 69.3% of US software development postings were senior-level. Only 4.5% were entry-level.

The detail: Indeed doesn't classify a posting as senior from its title or the years it asks for. It reads the responsibilities the posting describes.

So the market is literally sorting roles by scope, not tenure.

I think that's the right lens for our own careers too.

"5 years of React, Spring Boot and AWS" describes exposure. It doesn't describe what you were trusted to own: a ticket, a feature, a service, or a system other teams depend on.

The senior signals on public engineering ladders are fairly consistent:

• Decisions you owned, including the ones that turned out wrong
• Work that crossed team boundaries
• Incidents you were accountable for, not just paged into
• Engineers who got better because you were around
• Designs you wrote down before you built them

The last one is underrated. Plenty of engineers do real design work and never leave an artifact. If the reasoning only lives in a Slack thread, nobody can see the scope, including your next hiring manager.

AI makes this sharper, not softer. When producing code gets cheap, what's left to evaluate is judgment: what to build, what not to build, and how you'd know the output is right.

So the question I'm asking myself isn't "how many years do I have?"

It's "what's the largest thing I'd be trusted to own tomorrow, and where's the evidence?"

For those who hire: what's the clearest scope signal you look for that candidates rarely show?

#SoftwareEngineering #CareerGrowth #SystemDesign

posts.text:
🧱 From Boxes to Building Blocks 🧱

I've worked in software engineering, program management, business development, consulting, and IT recruitment. Looking back, tech was easier to sort into boxes. 📦 Software, hardware, and infrastructure mostly sat in the customer's own data center. It wasn't easy, but it was clear who owned what.

Then things shifted. Microsoft's "Software Plus Services" push, and later hybrid cloud, let companies keep some things in house and hand others to outside providers. What I first saw as fragmentation, I now see as specialization. 


🔍 Specialization Is Showing Up Everywhere 🔍

We build differently now, too. Tools like React help developers organize big, complex apps. Splitting applications into services creates clearer boundaries, though the complexity just moves into the connections between the pieces. 


🎓 Certifications Got More Specific 🎓

Certifications followed the same path. Labels like Java, Oracle, and PeopleSoft once covered a lot of ground. Today, Microsoft has moved from MCSA, MCSD, and MCSE to role based certifications, and Kubernetes has separate credentials for administration, development, and security. Expertise is now described in smaller, more precise pieces. 


💡 Why Certifications Still Matter Now 💡

When job requirements get specific, employers want clearer evidence of what someone knows. In the Linux Foundation's 2025 State of Tech Talent survey, 71% of organizations said certifications are important when evaluating technical skills. Hands on experience and portfolios ranked even higher, so think of a certification as a solid starting point, not the whole story. 


🤝 A Win for Recruiters 🤝

From my recruiting days, I can tell you this helps recruiters, too. "Cloud engineer" only tells you so much. A relevant certification helps a recruiter ask sharper screening questions, compare candidates to what the hiring manager needs, and spot where more assessment is needed. Just know what each credential covers, since a foundational cert and an implementation focused cert aren't the same. It's about matching evidence to the work, not counting badges. 


🏁 Make Your Skills Easy to Recognize 🏁

A certification won't erase onboarding, since knowing a platform isn't the same as knowing a company's systems and team habits. Even AWS says there's "no true substitute for experience." Still, a relevant cert plus recent project work can shorten the road to contributing. 🚀 

In a tough job market, pick certifications that fit the work you want, pair them with real examples of what you've built or improved, and share that story with confidence. 🙌 

Certifications give employers a clearer starting point and a credible case that you can do the work. ✨

Think about where this started.

A decision made with more hope than certainty. A first client that felt like a miracle. The early months of figuring everything out as you went. The nights you were not sure it was going to work, followed by the mornings you showed up anyway.

You built something from nothing. That is not a small thing.

But here is what often gets lost in the middle of building.

The same determination that got the business started can become the thing that keeps it from growing. Because effort alone, sustained indefinitely, without a clear financial picture, creates a ceiling. You can work harder and harder and still not break through it. Not because something is wrong with you, but because the business has outgrown the systems it started with.

At some point, working more is not the answer. Working with better information is.

When you can see your real profit margin, you can price with confidence. When you understand your cash flow, you can plan instead of react. When your financial picture is clear, you can make decisions about growth, hiring, and investment that are based on reality rather than instinct.

posts.text:
AI can write the code.
A good software engineer still has to know whether it should ship.
I use AI every day as a frontend developer.
It helps me learn faster and improve the way I work.
The judgment about what reaches production still stays with me.
𝟭. 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿?
Subscriptions, API usage, infrastructure, maintenance, and review time belong in the same calculation as hiring.
The leverage is real.
A lower total cost still has to be proven.
𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲?
When I ship incorrect code, my team investigates and owns the fix.
When AI generates that code and I merge it, responsibility stays with:
• The person who reviewed it
• The team that released it
• The company that set the process
The provider supplies the tool.
Shipping remains a human decision.
𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲?
Over the next five years, companies will look for engineers who can frame a problem, choose an architecture, review generated code, protect security, and maintain what they ship.
𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜 𝗮𝗺 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴
• Fundamentals: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, and the browser
• Problem framing and architecture
• Code review, debugging, and testing
• Security and product judgment
• Clear communication with design, product, and engineering
I plan to keep building these skills, use AI to learn faster, and understand every generated change before it reaches users.
I would like to hear your thoughts in the comments.
I respect your time, and I value every comment.

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄
1. Has AI reduced your overall cost of software development?
2. Who should be accountable when AI-generated code causes a production issue?
3. Which skills are you focusing on to stay valuable over the next five years?

💬 𝗟𝗲𝘁'𝘀 𝗸𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻. 😊 
There is a lot we can learn from each other. 👏

posts.text:
Recruiter: "So, do you know C?"

Me: "Yeah. I've been writing embedded C for about five years now."

Recruiter: "Great. And have you worked with React?"

Me: "..."

That little silence said a lot.

Look, I get it, recruiters juggle a hundred roles a day. But embedded hiring has this funny problem where the job and the interview sometimes feel like they're for two completely different roles.

The job is: bring up a board that's never booted before, chase a bug that shows up once a week and never the same way twice, make a CAN network behave, write a bootloader that must never brick a module.

The interview is: reverse a linked list on a whiteboard.

I'm not saying DSA doesn't matter. It does. But if you're hiring someone to debug real hardware, maybe ask them about the last board that didn't boot.

Embedded folks, what's the strangest question you've been asked in an interview for an embedded role?

posts.text:
We applaud recent graduates for taking time off to explore and reset. But when seasoned professionals step back for a year, we often react with skepticism instead of support. Why is that?

An employment gap isn’t a red flag—It can be a sign of strength.

It’s time to rethink how we view employment gaps when considering candidates.
Somehow, we’ve come to expect careers to run in a straight, unbroken line. When someone has a gap on their resume, the questions start: Why did they step away? What were they doing? Why weren’t they working?

But perhaps we're asking the wrong questions.

What if that gap shows someone recognized they were burned out or just needed a break to recharge? What if they made a conscious choice to focus on their mental health and well-being after decades of hard work?

That’s not weakness. If anything, it takes real strength.

We support young people who travel, try new things, and take time off before starting the next chapter. We know there’s value in stepping away for perspective.

So why don’t we offer the same understanding to experienced professionals?

Why judge someone who’s spent years working hard for taking some time for themselves?
Career breaks aren’t always about struggling to find work. Sometimes, they’re a thoughtful, planned choice—earned after years of effort.

Let’s be honest: it takes guts to realize you need a break and actually take one.

We say mental health and work-life balance matter. But when someone steps away to protect their well-being, they often face judgment when they return to work.

That doesn’t add up.

If you’re hiring, look past the dates on a resume.

A gap doesn’t mean someone lacks ambition or work ethic. It doesn’t erase years of experience or everything they bring to the table.

Instead of focusing on the gap, look at the whole person—their skills, experience, and what they offer now.

Careers are marathons, not sprints. Sometimes, a break is exactly what someone needs to come back stronger and more energized.

Let's stop treating employment gaps like red flags. People are more than the dates on their resume.

Taking a career break doesn’t mean you’ve lost your drive. Sometimes, it’s just realizing your well-being matters too.

That should never be held against anyone.

posts.text:
We moved millions of records from MySQL to PostgreSQL while 700,000 people kept using the system. Nobody noticed. And data now loads 3x faster. 🚀

It was a nationwide training center platform in Iraq, used every day, so shutting it down for a weekend wasn’t an option.

We didn’t just copy the tables over. We redesigned the schema along the way. Same data, better structure, and that alone made reads 3x faster.

How we did it without downtime:
 - Tested our backups first, by actually restoring them
 - Kept MySQL running and added Postgres next to it
 - Sent every new write to both databases
 - Moved old data in small batches with checkpoints, so a failed batch just re-ran on its own
 - Compared both databases, then moved reads to Postgres bit by bit
 - Kept MySQL live until the very end, just in case

✅ Zero downtime
✅ Zero data lost
⚡ 3x faster reads

Biggest lesson for me: a good migration is boring. Lots of small steps you can undo, no big dramatic switch.

I’m a full-stack engineer in Dubai (Node.js, NestJS, React) and I’m open to new roles. Happy to chat if you’re hiring. 👋

posts.text:
My wellness chatbot used to repeat itself. Here’s how I rebuilt it.
Rowl AI is a mental wellness app I built and deployed. Version 1 worked, but Sera, its chatbot, had real problems: it ran on a retired model, it fetched the oldest messages instead of the newest, and refreshing the page wiped the conversation.
So I rebuilt the core for Rowl AI 2.0:
🧠 Three layers of memory: recent messages, a short long-term summary, and the user’s profile with their latest journal mood
🔁 A three-model failover chain on Groq, so one dead model no longer breaks the chat
🛟 A crisis safeguard on both client and server: a persistent support banner with one-tap helpline buttons, a calming grounding screen (breathing voice, soft tones, a haptic pulse), and an optional alert email to a trusted contact
👩‍⚕️ A doctor dashboard with an AI-written pre-session brief
🔐 Password recovery with a 6-digit OTP
☁️ Graceful fallback when the database is unreachable
The biggest lesson: the unglamorous parts matter most. Failure handling, safe defaults, and what happens when something breaks at 2am are what make an app feel trustworthy.
Rowl is a self-care tool, not a substitute for professional help.
Built with React, Node/Express, MongoDB, Groq and Razorpay. I build with AI-assisted tools, and I’m making sure I can explain every layer.

posts.text:
The Miracle Morning:  Why Great Entrepreneurs Rush Slowly

The Reactive Trap

Most entrepreneurs start the day already behind. The phone lights up before the coffee does, an overnight email from a client, a cash-flow question from the bookkeeper, a team member who needs an answer now. Within minutes, we react instead of leading.

The Magic Morning

The most effective founders I work with protect what I call the "magic morning". The first 20 to 30 minutes of the day, before the world gets a vote. For many of them, the anchor is meditation.

Rush, Slowly

The Romans had a phrase for it. Festina lente, "make haste slowly." It sounds like a contradiction until you have run a business.  

MIT’s & MIG’s 
 
Old school, gain clarity on the Most Important Tasks and Most Important Goals that need to get done by simply jotting them down. Sure feels good checking them off, completing the day with that piece of paper in the trash can, ready for a fresh start tomorrow.

Power Down to Power Up

Think of your morning practice as powering down before the day powers up. Like a captain checking the instruments before leaving port, you are confirming your heading before the weather hits. 

You don't know what is coming to you today. A lost deal, a hiring crisis, an unexpected opportunity. You can decide who will be standing there when it arrives.

Then open the inbox. The day will still rush. You will just be the one setting the pace. 

#Pacing #Cadence #Clarity

posts.text:
He graduated from Princeton with perfect grades.

But his interviewer wasn’t impressed.

In the movie The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2012), Changez Khan interviews for a highly competitive financial analyst position at Underwood Samson.

He proudly explains that he’s never received a B and is about to graduate summa cum laude.

The interviewer, Jim Cross, barely reacts.

He’s already heard similar answers from several candidates that day.

Instead, Jim starts asking about Changez’s background, his financial struggles, and what motivates him.

Then comes the moment that changes the conversation.

Changez confidently tells him:

“Whether or not you hire me, Jim, I am going to win.”

The interviewer finally smiles.

What makes this scene interesting is the distinction between qualifications and motivation.

Academic achievements demonstrate discipline, intelligence, and consistency.

But they don’t necessarily reveal how someone responds to setbacks, handles uncertainty, or pursues difficult goals.

Great hiring decisions require understanding what candidates have accomplished and what drives them to accomplish more.

The strongest candidates bring more than impressive credentials.

They bring the determination to turn their potential into results.

#Leadership #Hiring #CareerDevelopment

🎬 Movie: The Reluctant Fundamentalist (2012)

261108 – Recently, a client complained to a coach, that the recruiter the client spoke to, was too abrasive. When I heard such a comment, I wondered to myself, “What is the purpose of the comment?”

Firstly, as job-seekers, our objective is to get the job. What we think of the recruiters, hiring managers, interviewers, or human recource personnels, is not important. Focus on what we need to do. We do not have to decide to turn down the offer, because we do not have the offer. We can withdraw our application, but have we assessed the opportunity thoroughly enough?

Secondly, when we watch the news, we focus on the news. We do not complain that the newscaster is being too negative. He/She is just reporting the news. We can choose not to watch the news when there is too much negativity. But for our job-hunt, we cannot afford to tune away, but only regulate ourselves accordingly.

In fact, we need to be conscious, are we emotionally affected by the news, or are we just unwilling to accept the truth? We can turn away temporarily. But to get to our goal, accepting the truth, and finding ways around it, is necessary.

Lastly, everything that we encounter is neutral. Positive or negative, is how we frame it. And in whatever that we do, focus on what we are trying to achieve, rather than being distracted by things around us. How we accept the things that we face, can help us to grow, developed our character, and make us better and stronger.

"Life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you react to it." The successful candidate who got the job, the colleague who got rewarded with a bonus and promotion, the pleasant service provider who got a superb review, the thriving business owner, they have their share of encounters with rude, nasty, abrasive, or even unreasonable individuals in their courses towards their goals. But they still thrive.

Do what is necessary, to get to where we want to be. There will be noises along the way. Tuning in to them, or shutting them off, is up to us. Our objective is to get to our goal, no matter what it takes.


=> we have an objective and a goal
=> there will be distractions around us
=> "Life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you react to it"
=> focus on our goal, and get to it, no matter what it takes

posts.text:
Every missed call is a patient who books with the next clinic. 📞 
So I built an AI receptionist for dental clinics, and it’s live. 😍 

It answers the phone in a natural voice, checks opening hours, and takes the booking request. The clinic’s staff then see the full transcript and a call summary in a private dashboard.
In the demo call, the caller asks for 12 AM. The assistant says the clinic is closed and offers 12 PM instead. The booking request lands on the schedule.
What’s under the hood:

→ Voice layer: Vapi (the call, speech and turn-taking)
→ Backend: Fastify + TypeScript, inputs validated with zod, webhook protected by a shared secret
→ Booking logic: opening hours, visit lengths and lead time in tested functions; Postgres advisory lock so two callers can’t take the same slot
→ Dashboard: Next.js 15 + React 19, signed-cookie login
→ Public demo reads a masked feed only: no phone numbers, no transcripts.

The clinic is fictional, but the build is real and you can try it yourself.
I’m a Senior Full Stack Engineer (React, Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, Python, Postgres, AWS) with 5+ years of experience. I’m open to remote contract roles, and I build AI assistants and web apps for small businesses.

If you’re hiring, or you run a clinic or service business that loses calls, send me a message.

posts.text:
99 cold emails in one inbox. 1 reply.

Watch the counter in the video.
It's one prospect's Monday morning.
(An illustration, but you've seen this inbox.)

99 emails say the same thing:
"Quick question about your growth."
Same tools. Same AI. Same template.

1 email says something else:
"Saw the hiring post for your new location. One idea for week one."

That's the one that got: "Good timing. Thursday?"

The difference isn't the writing.
It's knowing what just changed for them.

Doing that by hand takes hours a day.
So I built an AI system that does it for me:

1. Every morning it checks for signals
Job posts, funding rounds, new leaders, CRM switches.

2. AI checks each company against my ideal client
No fit, no email.

3. It writes one first line about what changed
Not "quick question". Not about me.

4. Replies land in my CRM with the signal attached
So I know why they answered before I open the email.

I still read every email before it goes out.
The system does the digging. I do the deciding.

Changing what I react to has moved my reply rates more than any copy tweak ever did.

The tools got cheaper.
Standing out didn't.

Comment SIGNAL and I'll show you how the system works.

posts.text:
Working in VA law enforcement gives us the privilege of serving a community that has already given so much.

Let’s face it, many of our Veterans have strong, Type A personalities. They’re direct, outspoken, independent, and not always interested in being told what to do. Some are dealing with pain, frustration, mental health challenges, or simply having a bad day. As VAP we’re going to be on the receiving end of that frustration.

Our job isn’t to win an argument. It’s to handle the situation professionally. Not every raised voice is a threat, not every disagreement is disrespect, and not every challenge to our authority requires a reaction.

When we allow our emotions to dictate our response, we risk escalating the situation, making the job harder for fellow officers and medical staff, and damaging the trust our community places in us. You can be firm without being disrespectful, assertive without being aggressive, and authoritative without being arrogant.

Professionalism doesn’t mean being a pushover. It means having the discipline, judgment, and emotional intelligence to know the difference between a genuine threat and someone who’s simply frustrated. We chose this profession, and with that comes a responsibility to uphold a higher standard, regardless of how others treat us.

Our Veterans don’t have to be easy to deal with to deserve dignity and professionalism.
Sometimes the greatest demonstration of authority is knowing when not to react.

Be firm. Be fair. Be accountable. Remember who we serve.

posts.text:
Junior devs, your LinkedIn headline is quietly costing you work.

"Full-stack web developer. HTML, CSS, JS, React, WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Python..."

You think that reads as versatile.
To the person hiring, it reads as "still figuring it out."

Here's the uncomfortable truth:
Nobody searches for a generalist.
They search for "fix my WooCommerce checkout."
"Move my site to Webflow CMS."
"Why is my Shopify store so slow?"

So pick one lane. Own it for 12 months.
Build three portfolio pieces that solve that exact problem.
Write about it here every single week.

It will feel like you're shrinking your options.
In reality, it's the moment people can finally find you.

Specialists get referred. Generalists get compared on price.

You can always widen later. Standing out on day one in a crowd of "I do everything" is the hard part.

If you had to pick ONE niche today, what would it be?

#WebDevelopment #FreelanceDeveloper #TechCareers #WordPress #CareerAdvice

posts.text:
So, what does it actually take to become an AI Engineer in 2026?

I'm not sure. Competition is growing, and so is demand. But one thing is clear: #AIengineering skills are becoming increasingly valuable, even outside traditionally technical roles.

As I was learning AI engineering skills myself, I wanted to know what the market actually needs, rather than just follow online learning roadmaps.

So I analysed the latest 1,488 AI Engineer job postings (with comparison to 6,160 SWE roles) across #Switzerland, #Germany, the #Netherlands and other European markets (July–November 2026). ( P.S. This was made possible by Jobfish.ing, a platform we've been building to help #jobhunters apply for the right opportunities in the fastest way. )

Three questions I want to answer for myself:
1. What skills are employers looking for in AI Engineers?
2. How do these differ from traditional Software Engineers?
3. Which industries are hiring AI Engineers?

Some takeaways:

1. LLMs are becoming standard. Python (75%), LLMs (69%), AI Agents (51%) and RAG (49%) are the most frequently mentioned skills. Around 80% of roles focus on building AI applications, while only ~12% involve model training or research. In other words, think software engineering with an LLM stack.

2. AI Engineer and SWE roles have distinct skill profiles:

More common in AI roles: LLMs, RAG, Python, AI Agents and Machine Learning.
Shared by both: Architecture/system design, CI/CD, security and privacy.
More common in SWE roles: Java, React, SQL databases, clean code/design patterns and Agile/Scrum.

I've included the full analysis in the pictures.

Curious to hear: What AI engineering skills are you prioritising in 2026?
