The data shows it—high-growth startups are 3x more likely to prioritize shipped work over pedigree. And honestly? It’s about time.

Location: Remote (India)
Type: Full-time / Long-term Contract
Email: hr@avantisofttech.com

About the Role
We are looking for an experienced Full-Stack Next.js / TypeScript Engineer to own technical maintenance, production reliability, and feature evolution for Statemento, a high-performance financial AI platform that converts complex bank statements into structured spreadsheets (Excel, CSV, QuickBooks).

Our entire stack is built in a modern, unified TypeScript ecosystem—no context-switching between backend languages. You will work directly on serverless architecture, AI extraction pipelines, database integrity, and webhook-driven billing systems.

What You’ll Do
Maintain & Scale the Core App: Own full-stack development across our Next.js App Router, React Server/Client Components, and Node.js serverless runtimes.

Refine AI Extraction Pipelines: Maintain and optimize document parsing workflows using LLM APIs (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI) and local PDF text processors (unpdf), ensuring strict balance reconciliation and zero data leakage.

Database & Auth Operations: Manage PostgreSQL on Supabase, write and deploy schema migrations, enforce strict Row-Level Security (RLS) policies, and debug connection pooling.

Payment & Subscription Lifecycle: Maintain our Merchant of Record integrations (Lemon Squeezy), including webhook event listeners, signature validation, idempotency guards, and customer entitlement syncs.

Production Reliability & Bug Triage: Monitor application health across Vercel, Supabase, and Upstash Redis. Diagnose and resolve edge-case PDF conversion issues and balance check discrepancies.

Testing & Code Quality: Run and expand automated test suites using TypeScript and Node’s native test runner (tsx).

What We’re Looking For
3–6 years of professional software engineering experience, with substantial production experience in TypeScript and modern Next.js (App Router).

Strong Database Fundamentals: Hands-on experience with PostgreSQL, schema design, and Supabase (specifically writing secure RLS policies).

Serverless & Webhook Proficiency: Solid understanding of stateless API design, HMAC signature verification, idempotency patterns, and asynchronous error boundaries.

Low-Level Data Handling: Comfortable working with Node.js streams, buffers (Uint8Array), and file transformations (CSV, XLSX).

Autonomous Problem Solver: High ownership mindset

Our Tech Stack
Frontend & Backend: Next.js (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
Data & Storage: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Upstash Redis (rate limiting)
Hosting & Runtime: Vercel Edge/Serverless, Node.js 24
AI & Document Processing: Anthropic Claude API, OpenAI API, unpdf, write-excel-file

posts.text:
A REQUEST TO RECRUITERS & HR PROFESSIONALS 🙏

Dear Recruiters, HR Professionals and Hiring Managers,

Please understand the feelings of job seekers.

When you publish a job vacancy on LinkedIn, many people react, comment and show interest. Some candidates politely comment, "Please share your resume."

Job seekers trust your words, prepare their CVs and send their resumes with hope of getting an opportunity.

But unfortunately, after receiving the resume, many recruiters don't respond. No interview call, no rejection message, not even a simple update.

Please remember:

- A job seeker's time is valuable.
- Every resume represents someone's hope and hard work.
- Not every candidate will be selected, and that's absolutely fine.
- But a simple response can make a big difference.
- If a candidate is not suitable, please communicate it politely.

You don't have to give everyone a job, but you can give everyone a response.

Behind every resume, there is a person waiting for an opportunity, someone working hard to support their family and build a better future.

Respect job seekers. Respect their time. Respect their hopes.

Let's make LinkedIn a platform for genuine opportunities, not just collecting resumes.

#JobSeekers #LinkedIn #Recruitment #HRProfessionals #Hiring #JobOpportunities #CareerGrowth #RespectJobSeekers #Recruiter #ProfessionalEthics

posts.text:
I built my own Vercel from scratch. 🚀
You sign in with GitHub, pick a Vite/React repo, and the platform builds it in an isolated AWS Fargate container. Build logs stream live to your browser, and the site goes live at <slug>.yourdomain.com. A git push redeploys it automatically.
Under the hood it’s 10 backend services in a TypeScript monorepo, using Express, Postgres, Redis, BullMQ, Kafka, ClickHouse, S3 and Socket.IO. These were the parts that taught me the most:
🔒 One active build per user. A Redis lock stores the owning deployment ID and is released with a Lua compare-and-delete. A late cancel can never free a lock that now belongs to someone else. Postgres compare-and-set updates mean a cancelled deploy can never flip back to “ready”.
📡 Live logs with no gaps or duplicates. Container → Kafka → two consumer groups. One fans out over Socket.IO and the other persists to ClickHouse. Every event carries a per-deployment sequence number. The browser subscribes first, then fetches history, then merges by sequence.
🔑 Auth that assumes tokens get stolen. Refresh tokens rotate on every use. If an old one is replayed, an atomic Lua script detects it and revokes the whole session.
🛡️ Safer builds. User code runs with a minimal environment, so platform secrets are never visible to it. Secrets are redacted from every log line, including URL-encoded and base64 forms.
The biggest lesson: the happy path is the easy part. The real design work is in cancellations, crashes, retries, duplicate webhooks and Kafka outages.
I’m a final-year B.Tech student looking for Software Engineer roles in India. If you’re hiring, or just want to talk distributed systems, I’d love to connect.

posts.text:
New here, or been reading all week? One post about working with me — then back to the useful stuff.

I am Muhammad Hamad, a Full Stack Developer and AI Engineer with 8 years of experience, working remotely with clients and teams worldwide.

Most good projects I have seen do not start with "build us an AI system". They start with one workflow that wastes a team's week.

So here is how working with me usually starts:

1. You describe the workflow that wastes your team's time — leads, data entry, follow-ups, documents, support.
2. I tell you honestly whether AI, automation, or simple software is the right fix — including when the answer is "do not build anything yet".
3. We start narrow: one task, clear rules, a human checking the important steps. Then we expand only if it works.

What I build around that first step: workflow automation, AI features and agents with rules and limits you control, and the software around them — SaaS platforms, dashboards, and internal tools.

My stack: Python, TypeScript, React, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI — plus OpenAI and Claude APIs, LangChain, and retrieval systems.

Two ways to start a conversation:
- Businesses: message me the workflow. I will reply with the first step I would take.
- Recruiters and hiring managers: message me the role. My portfolio and experience are at hamadshafiq.com.

No pressure, no pitch beyond this post. Tomorrow we go back to teaching.

Which workflow would you bring to that first conversation?

posts.text:
One bug in our SkilledCoder test let anyone take over any user’s account.

It was one of 6 bugs we planted in a realistic login system. Last night I ran a full walkthrough of the test to see exactly what a candidate sees.

The candidate gets an AI assistant, just like at work. But the AI won’t find the bug for you. You have to find it, tell the AI exactly what to fix, and explain why it broke.

My report: 86 out of 100, 5 of 6 bugs fixed. It scored my efficiency 43 and told me to give the AI one clear, specific instruction up front.

That’s the skill now. AI can write the fix. The engineer has to know what’s wrong and what the fix should be.

Last week 48 engineers signed up and 36 took a test. Most ran out of the 60 minute clock.

If you hire engineers, this is the skill worth testing for.

Engineers, suggest our next challenge. Reply with stack + bug, like:
Go: two workers pick up the same job
Node: users still see old data after an update
React: form submits twice on a double click

The most requested one gets built next.

Try it free: skilledcoder.ai/practice

Happy Diwali  🪔

Here is the October 2026 update for the Hacker News "Who's Hiring" index.

545 job postings in October, up from 539 in September and down from 796 in October last year. Median pay went down to $185k, from $195k.

• July, August, September and October were the four quietest months in over 12 years. There have been 6,400 postings so far this year, 12% fewer than the same months of 2025.
• In 11 of the previous 14 years, October had more postings than September. This year it had 6 more.
• Remote roles paid a median of $170k and onsite roles $219k. Remote has paid less than onsite every month since February. From October 2025 to January 2026 remote paid more. Half of all posted salaries were between $165k and $220k.
• TypeScript, Python and React were the most-requested skills. About 1 in 5 postings asked for an AI or machine learning skill, about the same as September. Claude Code was the AI coding tool named most often, as it has been every month since March.
• Remote was 48% of roles, hybrid 24% and onsite 28%. Remote has been between 45% and 53% every month for the past year. UK roles went from 33 to 58, the most since June.
• Engineering was 61% of postings. In October 2024 it was 74%. Data and ML went from 12% to 15% over the same two years.
The November update will be out in early December.

posts.text:
Enjoying a quiet Sunday coffee and thinking back to the 2021 hiring freeze.

Our Jakarta pipeline was exploding, my budget was locked, and HR wasn't allowed to approve a single new headcount.

So my Sales Director and I told Finance we were starting an "internship program" and brought in a Toyota car salesman, a Uniqlo retail worker, a graphic designer, and a chef who was also a barber to sell Google Cloud.

Tomorrow morning at 7 AM SGT on "Kitchen Counter CEO", I am sharing what happened three months later (and why most CEOs get "wildcard" hiring completely wrong). ☕

posts.text:
URGENTLY HIRING, BUT NOT URGENT ENOUGH TO UPDATE CANDIDATES?

Ada satu hal yang menurut saya perlu menjadi perhatian lebih banyak perusahaan di Indonesia yaitu candidate experience.

Kita sering melihat perusahaan berlomba-lomba membangun employer branding, memamerkan budaya kerja, mengusung slogan people first, dan menyatakan bahwa karyawan adalah aset paling berharga bagi perusahaan.

Namun, apakah nilai-nilai tersebut benar-benar tercermin dari cara perusahaan memperlakukan kandidat selama proses rekrutmen?

Tidak sedikit kandidat yang harus meluangkan waktu untuk menyiapkan CV, mengisi berbagai formulir, mengerjakan psikotes, mengikuti FGD, interview HR, interview user, bahkan melewati beberapa tahapan seleksi lainnya.

Sayangnya, setelah seluruh proses tersebut, tidak sedikit yang justru berakhir dengan ketidakpastian.

Tidak ada kabar. Tidak ada pembaruan. Bahkan tidak ada pemberitahuan bahwa kandidat sudah tidak lagi dipertimbangkan.

Pertanyaannya sederhana, sesulit itukah memberikan satu email atau pesan singkat untuk menginformasikan hasil seleksi?

Perlu dipahami bahwa rekrutmen adalah proses dua arah. Perusahaan memang berhak memilih kandidat terbaik, tetapi kandidat juga sedang menginvestasikan waktu, tenaga, dan ekspektasi mereka kepada perusahaan.

Tidak semua kandidat harus diterima, tetapi setiap kandidat berhak mendapatkan komunikasi yang profesional.

Memberikan kabar bahwa kandidat belum lolos bukanlah sesuatu yang sulit. Begitu pula memberikan informasi jika proses rekrutmen masih berlangsung atau mengalami penundaan.

Hal sederhana seperti ini justru dapat membangun kesan positif terhadap perusahaan.

Ingat, candidate experience juga merupakan bagian dari employer branding.

Kandidat yang hari ini kalian abaikan bisa saja menjadi pelanggan, mitra bisnis, atau bahkan talenta potensial yang suatu saat dibutuhkan perusahaan.

Jika perusahaan menuntut profesionalisme dari kandidat, bukankah sudah seharusnya perusahaan menunjukkan profesionalisme yang sama?

Pada akhirnya, proses rekrutmen bukan hanya tentang bagaimana perusahaan memilih kandidat, tetapi juga bagaimana perusahaan memperlakukan manusia di balik setiap CV yang diterima.

#CandidateExperience #EmployerBranding #Recruitment #HumanResources #Karier

Looking for skilled UAV Design & Development Engineer with strong expertise in aircraft conceptual design, preliminary sizing, aerodynamic configuration and 3D CAD modelling. The candidate will be responsible for designing and developing fixed-wing, VTOL and multirotor UAV platforms, from conceptualisation and sizing to detailed CAD design and prototype development.

Key Responsibilities
Perform conceptual and preliminary design of UAV platforms.
Carry out aircraft sizing, including weight estimation, payload capacity, range, endurance and performance calculations.
Develop aerodynamic configurations for fixed-wing, delta-wing, quadplane and multirotor UAVs.
Perform wing sizing, airfoil selection, aspect ratio optimisation and aerodynamic analysis.
Calculate thrust-to-weight ratio, wing loading, power requirements and propulsion system sizing.
Design fuselage, wings, tail structures, control surfaces, landing gear and payload integration systems.
Develop detailed 3D CAD models, assemblies, engineering drawings and manufacturing-ready designs.
Perform structural design and preliminary load calculations.
Coordinate with CFD, FEA, propulsion, avionics and manufacturing teams.
Support prototype fabrication, assembly, integration and flight testing.
Optimise UAV designs for weight, performance, manufacturability and operational reliability.
Required Technical Skills
Strong understanding of aircraft design, aerodynamics and flight mechanics.
Experience in UAV sizing and performance estimation.
Proficiency in 3D CAD software such as CATIA, SolidWorks, Siemens NX or Creo.
Knowledge of aircraft structures, materials and lightweight design.
Understanding of propulsion system selection and integration (electric motors, batteries, engines and hybrid propulsion).
Ability to prepare detailed engineering drawings, BOMs and manufacturing documentation.
Preferred Skills
Experience designing fixed-wing, delta-wing, VTOL and multirotor UAVs.
Knowledge of CFD tools such as ANSYS Fluent, STAR-CCM+ or OpenFOAM.
Experience with FEA and structural analysis using ANSYS or equivalent tools.
Knowledge of flight dynamics, stability and control.
Familiarity with MATLAB, Python and aircraft sizing tools.
Experience in prototype development and actual UAV flight testing.

B.Tech / M.Tech/PhD in Aerospace Engineering, and Aeronautical Engineering 

Ideal Candidate

posts.text:
Years of experience is a lagging indicator. Scope is the signal.

I've been reading Indeed Hiring Lab's July report on seniority, and one methodology detail stuck with me more than the headline number.

The headline: in Q1 2026, 69.3% of US software development postings were senior-level. Only 4.5% were entry-level.

The detail: Indeed doesn't classify a posting as senior from its title or the years it asks for. It reads the responsibilities the posting describes.

So the market is literally sorting roles by scope, not tenure.

I think that's the right lens for our own careers too.

"5 years of React, Spring Boot and AWS" describes exposure. It doesn't describe what you were trusted to own: a ticket, a feature, a service, or a system other teams depend on.

The senior signals on public engineering ladders are fairly consistent:

• Decisions you owned, including the ones that turned out wrong
• Work that crossed team boundaries
• Incidents you were accountable for, not just paged into
• Engineers who got better because you were around
• Designs you wrote down before you built them

The last one is underrated. Plenty of engineers do real design work and never leave an artifact. If the reasoning only lives in a Slack thread, nobody can see the scope, including your next hiring manager.

AI makes this sharper, not softer. When producing code gets cheap, what's left to evaluate is judgment: what to build, what not to build, and how you'd know the output is right.

So the question I'm asking myself isn't "how many years do I have?"

It's "what's the largest thing I'd be trusted to own tomorrow, and where's the evidence?"

For those who hire: what's the clearest scope signal you look for that candidates rarely show?

#SoftwareEngineering #CareerGrowth #SystemDesign

Your competitors don't need better employees.

They need better systems.

And AI is making that difference impossible to ignore.

Imagine opening your laptop tomorrow morning.

Your competitors have already:

→ Identified promising leads.

→ Analyzed customer feedback.

→ Prepared personalized proposals.

→ Flagged emerging market trends.

→ Generated their weekly performance reports.

Not because their teams worked all night.

Because their workflows kept running.

That's the real promise of AI agents.

Not another chatbot that waits for instructions.

But software that can execute defined tasks, use connected tools, and coordinate multiple steps with appropriate oversight.

Here's where it gets interesting.

Most businesses are still asking:

"Which AI tool should we buy?"

A better question is:

"Which process should we redesign?"

Because adding AI to a broken workflow doesn't automatically fix it.

It can simply make mistakes happen faster.

Start with one process.

Define the desired outcome.

Connect the necessary tools.

Establish approval checkpoints.

Measure the results.

Then improve.

The next competitive advantage won't necessarily come from hiring more people or buying more software.

It may come from making existing resources dramatically more effective.

AI isn't just changing how we work.

It's changing what a small, well-organized team can accomplish.

And that should get every business leader thinking.

What's the first workflow you'd delegate to an AI agent?

We ship 11 apps with a team of zero. Here is the technical architecture of the 'Marketing OS' we built to handle our distribution.

Running eleven apps across Android, iOS, and Wear OS is a product challenge, but marketing them is a logistics one. Instead of hiring, we built an automated pipeline that handles research, rendering, and performance learning.

First, we capture real gameplay and app footage using emulators rather than physical devices. This allows us to scale recording for games like Rope Ninja and Loo Lord without a studio setup. These raw clips are fed into a central asset library.

Our system uses a series of LLM agents for the creative work. One agent researches platform trends and audience pain points. A second agent writes the copy based on our historical A/B data—like knowing that 'expensive hardware vs basic software' hooks win for Watchland. A third agent then generates the video scenes and lifestyle backdrops.

The final renders are queued through Buffer for posting across six platforms. The loop closes when the system pulls engagement data back into its learning model.

Last month, this system generated 212,280 views across our portfolio. While the conversion to installs varies—Meme Soundboard saw 111,000 views turn into only 8 installs—the system allows us to test hundreds of hooks that a human team wouldn't have the time to write.

For solo founders, the bottleneck isn't usually code. It is the friction of repeating the same marketing tasks. We built this to solve our own friction.

If you are building a multi-app portfolio, how are you handling the distribution side without a dedicated team?

🚨 The AI Advantage in Cybersecurity is a Double-Edged Sword 🚨

A recent McKinsey report highlights a critical reality for businesses: Frontier AI is dramatically accelerating how quickly cyberattackers can identify and exploit software vulnerabilities.

The window to defend is slamming shut. Previously, the average time between a critical vulnerability disclosure and active exploitation was a few weeks. Today, it is just a matter of hours.

Despite this, organizations are falling behind. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report analysis notes that the median time taken by organizations to fully remediate vulnerabilities has actually increased from 32 days to 43 days. By 2026, roughly two-thirds of exploited vulnerabilities were being attacked on or before the day they were even disclosed.

AI’s bug-finding scale is unprecedented. For context, Anthropic’s Project Glasswing used Claude Mythos Preview to identify over 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities, increasing bug-finding rates more than tenfold.

So, how do companies adapt? McKinsey emphasizes that simply hiring more security personnel or trying to patch faster won’t be enough. Organizations must fundamentally overhaul four core areas:

1️⃣ Cybersecurity Practices: Implement automated, continuous security monitoring and introduce secure development practices. 

2️⃣ Operating Models: Establish clear accountability for vulnerabilities and regularly monitor third-party suppliers. 

3️⃣ Risk and Control Frameworks: Strengthen identity and access controls, particularly over AI-powered systems. 

4️⃣ Technology: Shift to an integrated security program that combines automated discovery and prioritization with human oversight.

The report recommends starting with a 90-day rollout of this new framework, beginning with critical systems and expanding based on measurable improvements.

-  Software: licenses and subscriptions for each new user

-  Security: secure setup and cybersecurity training
-  IT support: time spent configuring devices and accounts
-  Capacity: additional storage, infrastructure and support as the team grows

🚀 Mechcraft 2.0 update is live — GPS Walking Mode + Full-Stack AWS Cloud Integration!
As software engineers, it’s far too easy to stay locked behind a screen and forget to get our daily steps in. I do a ton of walking and love location-based games like Pokémon GO and Monster Hunter Now — but I got tired of the paywalls and microtransactions.
So, I built my own walking game mode into Mechcraft instead! 🛠️🚶‍♂️

☁️ Why I Built the Backend on AWS:
Almost every engineering role today asks for hands-on AWS experience. The challenge? Most enterprise cloud architectures we build at work are proprietary, protected under strict NDAs, and impossible to showcase in a public portfolio.
With Mechcraft 2.0, I built a complete, production cloud backend that serves as 100% public, unencumbered proof of my cloud engineering capabilities:
•
AWS Lambda & EventBridge: Scheduled serverless cron workflows for automated 5-minute passive resource accrual.
•
Amazon DynamoDB: Low-latency state persistence, real-time balance tracking, and optimistic concurrency management.
•
REST / Serverless APIs: Seamless real-time sync between iOS client actions and cloud services.
🎮 What’s New in Mechcraft 2.0:
📍 Real-World GPS Exploration: Your Drillbot tracks your physical coordinates on a custom tactical MapKit HUD. Explore your neighborhood to scan sectors and harvest Mineral & Gas nodes.
⚔️ Cross-Mode Progression & Shared Rewards: No siloed gameplay. Every resource, guard tower, and upgrade you gather while walking feeds directly into your RTS fleet and battle stages.
🎁 Map Surprises & Tactical POIs: Discover defense points, dynamic resource caches, and sector secrets as you hit your step targets.
💡 The Big Takeaway:
There’s nothing better than building something you use every single day, saving money on mobile games, getting healthier, and creating tangible, public architectural evidence of modern cloud engineering in the process.
If you’re hiring for iOS / Cloud / AWS roles or just want to chat about combining MapKit, SceneKit, and AWS serverless architecture, feel free to reach out or connect!

posts.text:
What happens when companies need experienced workers but stop hiring beginners?

I have been thinking about this question while reading research from Stanford.

In an August 2026 update, researchers examining US payroll data found that employment among 22–25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations was approximately 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with their less-exposed peers.

Interestingly, the difference appeared primarily through reduced hiring, rather than increased layoffs.

The researchers caution that this does not establish AI as the cause.

But the finding raises a question that goes beyond today's employment numbers.

Consider how people become experienced professionals.

A junior software developer learns by writing code, fixing defects, and understanding why systems fail. A young analyst develops judgment by examining data, making mistakes, and learning from feedback.

These activities are not merely tasks to be completed. They are also how professional expertise develops.

If organisations increasingly automate such work, they may improve immediate productivity while unintentionally reducing opportunities for beginners to gain experience.

That creates a possible long-term problem.

Companies may eventually need experienced professionals without having invested enough in developing them.

Perhaps the next important question about AI and employment is not simply how many jobs technology can replace.

It is who will develop tomorrow's experienced workers if fewer people are given the opportunity to begin.

Source: Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 12 August 2026.

posts.text:
Four things to remember about job hunting and interviewing in uncertain times:

1. Great feedback is not a job offer.

You can nail every round and the role can still get pulled. "Did they like me?" and "Can they actually hire?" are two completely different things. So, never pause your search just because an interview went well.

2. Talk to people who just left.

Current employees get hit up all day. Their inboxes are full.
Find someone good who left 3 to 6 months ago using LinkedIn - I know this will take time, which is exactly why you should do it. Ask them what the team was really like. If you connect with them, they won't send you an application link. They’ll text their old boss directly. That could be your next interview right there. 

3. Ask about their cash.

You need to interview them just as hard as they interview you. If you're interviewing with start ups, sak how much runway they actually have left. Ask what happens if they miss their revenue numbers this year. Getting laid off 6 months down the line in is something you could have potentially spot early.

4. Go after the boring companies.

Everyone is fighting 1,000 other people for the same shiny AI startups.
Look at logistics software. Look at payment infrastructure. Look at unsexy B2B tools that print cash. Less hype and possibly way fewer applicants to compete with. 

Bonus tip: if you have LinkedIn Premium, check the company’s Insights tab before your next interview. Scroll down to "Total job openings" and look at the 3-month and 6-month growth trends by department. If a hiring manager tells you they’re aggressively scaling, but their engineering openings are flat over 3 months and down 58% over the last six. Trust the real headcount data over the interview pitch, I'd say. 

I know that doesn't sound exciting and it does sound like a second job. But it works and it's what's necessary in this market right now.

Put the right people in the right roles, and you're far less likely to be replacing them a few months later.

That work starts before the offer.

People who use their strengths every day are six times more likely to be engaged at work, according to Gallup. That's research about employees already in roles, not a promise about a new hire. But it raises a useful hiring question:

Will this role give someone the chance to do what they do best?

Start with the work, not just the job title.

What will they spend most of their week doing? Which tasks need someone who loves detail, solves unfamiliar problems or brings people together?

Then make the hiring process reflect that work. Choose a skills assessment relevant to the tasks. Ask referees for examples of when the candidate did similar work well, and where they needed support.

Use those answers to explore the match, not to put someone in a fixed box.

The goal isn't simply to fill a seat. It's to give a capable person the right work, with clear expectations, before the offer goes out.

posts.text:
🧱 From Boxes to Building Blocks 🧱

I've worked in software engineering, program management, business development, consulting, and IT recruitment. Looking back, tech was easier to sort into boxes. 📦 Software, hardware, and infrastructure mostly sat in the customer's own data center. It wasn't easy, but it was clear who owned what.

Then things shifted. Microsoft's "Software Plus Services" push, and later hybrid cloud, let companies keep some things in house and hand others to outside providers. What I first saw as fragmentation, I now see as specialization. 


🔍 Specialization Is Showing Up Everywhere 🔍

We build differently now, too. Tools like React help developers organize big, complex apps. Splitting applications into services creates clearer boundaries, though the complexity just moves into the connections between the pieces. 


🎓 Certifications Got More Specific 🎓

Certifications followed the same path. Labels like Java, Oracle, and PeopleSoft once covered a lot of ground. Today, Microsoft has moved from MCSA, MCSD, and MCSE to role based certifications, and Kubernetes has separate credentials for administration, development, and security. Expertise is now described in smaller, more precise pieces. 


💡 Why Certifications Still Matter Now 💡

When job requirements get specific, employers want clearer evidence of what someone knows. In the Linux Foundation's 2025 State of Tech Talent survey, 71% of organizations said certifications are important when evaluating technical skills. Hands on experience and portfolios ranked even higher, so think of a certification as a solid starting point, not the whole story. 


🤝 A Win for Recruiters 🤝

From my recruiting days, I can tell you this helps recruiters, too. "Cloud engineer" only tells you so much. A relevant certification helps a recruiter ask sharper screening questions, compare candidates to what the hiring manager needs, and spot where more assessment is needed. Just know what each credential covers, since a foundational cert and an implementation focused cert aren't the same. It's about matching evidence to the work, not counting badges. 


🏁 Make Your Skills Easy to Recognize 🏁

A certification won't erase onboarding, since knowing a platform isn't the same as knowing a company's systems and team habits. Even AWS says there's "no true substitute for experience." Still, a relevant cert plus recent project work can shorten the road to contributing. 🚀 

In a tough job market, pick certifications that fit the work you want, pair them with real examples of what you've built or improved, and share that story with confidence. 🙌 

Certifications give employers a clearer starting point and a credible case that you can do the work. ✨

Happy Diwali to those who celebrate! Diwali is about light and new beginnings, and that’s a pretty good summary of my last few months

When I left AWS, I said eight years flew by. Since then I’ve joined DDN in a leadership role across Product and BizOps. Data Direct Networks is the data platform behind some of the world’s largest AI factories, and it runs with startup energy. We’re now helping next-gen neoclouds get every ounce of performance out of their GPUs. The last two months have gone even faster: new hire orientation and QBR in NYC, Nvidia GTC in Berlin, and many customer engagements.

Huge thanks to  Kevin Delane & Omer Asad for the opportunity. DDN has also felt like a homecoming, with so many Pure Storage folks Wes van den Berg, Andy LeSage, Gary Kortye, Andrew "AJ" Shiekman  who made my ramp-up easy. Any many many new colleagues in engineering: Massimo Francato, Chris Schin, Andrew Murphy, Sanjay Jagad, Ravindra S., Ashutosh Mate mate: thanks for the warm welcome!

The AI conversation has flipped fast. A year ago it was “how much compute can I get?” Now it’s “how efficiently can I use it?” Customers are tuning the whole stack, from GPUs and networking to storage and software. More and more, data is the bottleneck, and that’s exactly where DDN shines !

The fun part: we’ve got a king-of-the-hill market leading product and an early-stage one crossing the chasm. One is about defending leadership and scaling growth, and the other is about earning every early win. My biggest lesson so far is that you cross the chasm one customer at a time, by starting from their problem, not your product.

And if you see an exciting role at DDN, send me a note. We’re hiring!

posts.text:
Too many hiring processes confuse experience with relevance.

Someone who has spent twenty years translating complex technical systems into practical learning solutions does not suddenly become incapable because the technology changes from:
- Air traffic management
- Rail signalling
- Defence communications

to:
- Mining software
- ERP platforms
- Customer applications

The domain changes.
The learning problem often doesn’t.

You still need to understand the system, identify what people need to do differently, work with subject matter experts, design the right support, and help people become competent and confident using something new.

If a hiring process only recognises exact industry or keyword matches, it may be reducing one kind of risk while creating another: filtering out people who are very good at learning unfamiliar domains quickly.

posts.text:
"Technical leader, people leader, AI orchestrator: the false choice every EM is being asked to make"

"Will the engineering manager of 2030 be a technical leader, a people leader, or an AI orchestrator?” is a well-meaning question built on a false premise. The data coming out right now says the answer isn’t “which one” — it’s all 3.

Here’s what’s already happening, not speculation about 2030:
💻 The “non-technical EM” is already disappearing
Industry survey data from 2026 shows the share of engineering managers doing hands-on technical work jumped from 20% to 35% in a single year. Tech leads, CTOs, and managers of managers all show the same pattern — more time coding and reviewing, not less. The “player-coach” model that was a prediction a couple of years ago is now the measured norm. 

📊 Organizations are flattening, and spans are widening — maybe too fast
As AI absorbs status reporting and coordination busywork, companies are using that slack to remove manager layers and widen how many people each remaining manager leads. The logic sounds reasonable. But practitioners are already flagging the catch: AI increases the volume of code changes needing review and judgment faster than it reduces coordination overhead. Widening a manager’s span because “AI makes everyone more productive” risks optimising the wrong bottleneck entirely.

🤖 “AI orchestrator” is quietly forking into two different jobs
Job postings today use “AI engineering manager” to mean two genuinely different roles: a domain-specialized EM leading human AI/ML engineers, or a newer shape entirely — someone leading a handful of humans plus fleets of AI agents spread across several teams. 

🎯 Hiring bars already have a sixth axis for this
Engineering manager interview rubrics at major companies added a new evaluation dimension in 2026 specifically for AI: not just “do you use AI tools,” but can you review AI-generated code for architectural and security issues, and can you challenge inflated productivity claims using real delivery metrics instead of taking self-reported gains at face value.

😬 The honest risk nobody’s pricing in
AI removed real overhead from the EM role — but it added new categories of work: reviewing agent output, defending metrics with evidence, deciding what goes to a person vs. an agent. The “AI frees up manager time” story is only half true. 

So who’s actually at risk by 2030?
Not the non-technical EM alone, and not the AI-skeptical EM alone. The real “dead zone” is a specific combination: one team, 6–9 people, no technical depth to earn credibility, no agent-orchestration skill to justify a wider span. That configuration is getting squeezed from both directions — flattening removes the role, and agentic team structures don’t need a pure coordinator either.

The uncomfortable implication: by 2030, “engineering manager” might not describe one job with a widening job description. It might describe two or three distinct jobs that currently share a title.

posts.text:
Years of experience is a lagging indicator. Scope is the signal.

I've been reading Indeed Hiring Lab's July report on seniority, and one methodology detail stuck with me more than the headline number.

The headline: in Q1 2026, 69.3% of US software development postings were senior-level. Only 4.5% were entry-level.

The detail: Indeed doesn't classify a posting as senior from its title or the years it asks for. It reads the responsibilities the posting describes.

So the market is literally sorting roles by scope, not tenure.

I think that's the right lens for our own careers too.

"5 years of React, Spring Boot and AWS" describes exposure. It doesn't describe what you were trusted to own: a ticket, a feature, a service, or a system other teams depend on.

The senior signals on public engineering ladders are fairly consistent:

• Decisions you owned, including the ones that turned out wrong
• Work that crossed team boundaries
• Incidents you were accountable for, not just paged into
• Engineers who got better because you were around
• Designs you wrote down before you built them

The last one is underrated. Plenty of engineers do real design work and never leave an artifact. If the reasoning only lives in a Slack thread, nobody can see the scope, including your next hiring manager.

AI makes this sharper, not softer. When producing code gets cheap, what's left to evaluate is judgment: what to build, what not to build, and how you'd know the output is right.

So the question I'm asking myself isn't "how many years do I have?"

It's "what's the largest thing I'd be trusted to own tomorrow, and where's the evidence?"

For those who hire: what's the clearest scope signal you look for that candidates rarely show?

#SoftwareEngineering #CareerGrowth #SystemDesign

posts.text:
The yacht you want is not hiring your ambition.
It is hiring your readiness.

When a captain or head of department opens a stack of applications between watches, "experienced crew member" tells them almost nothing. Experienced where? On what programme? Carrying which responsibilities? And who can confirm it?

YPI CREW's recruitment guidance keeps coming back to the same short list: an up-to-date CV, certificates clearly listed, visa status stated, availability confirmed, and a track record someone can check.

None of that is glamorous. All of it is decisive.

Watch how the same experience disappears on paper:

A deckhand writes "confident tender driver", when the real story is two Med seasons of guest transfers on a 55m, with Powerboat Level 2 and PWC tickets dated and in date.

An engineer writes "maintained all systems", when the chief wants to know which generators, which watermakers, and whether there was a yard period behind it.

A chief stew writes "managed the interior team", when the captain needs to know: how many people, charter or private, and for how long.

Nothing in those rewrites inflates the career. They simply stop the reader from having to guess.

And the market is not one market. A busy window for junior deck says nothing about demand for second engineers or head chefs. Being active is not the same as being relevant.

Your strongest application is the one that answers the questions behind the vacancy before anyone has to ask them.

If a captain opened your CV this morning, would your relevance be obvious, or would they have to piece it together?

Want an outside read on how your CV answers those questions?

posts.text:
Are we hiring experts, or building an organisation that creates them?
 
Technology has a curious relationship with talent.
 
We celebrate the exceptional engineer. The brilliant architect. The coding prodigy. The person who seems to have an answer for everything.
 
Our hiring language often suggests technical excellence is innate: something rare we must find, rather than a capability we can develop.
 
Recent Rotman research challenges that assumption (link in comments). It contrasts the “creative genius”, whose talent is rare and innate, with the “creative explorer”, whose creativity grows through curiosity, experimentation and learning.
 
Genius language dominated more than 9,000 job postings for creative roles. Yet with real job seekers, explorer language attracted more applicants, especially the curious, open-minded people organisations most want.
 
That matters in technology.
 
The best engineers I’ve worked with didn’t always know the most at the start. They knew how to investigate what they didn’t understand, challenge assumptions, learn from failure and connect ideas across disciplines.
 
Here’s where I’d go further: AI adds a complication.
 
AI can now write code, generate tests, explain errors and suggest architectures. Those tasks are also how engineers develop judgement.
 
A junior engineer who hands every debugging exercise to AI may deliver faster, but miss learning how systems actually fail. An architect who accepts an AI-generated design without questioning it may produce a convincing blueprint without understanding the system.
 
This isn’t an argument against automation. It’s an argument for being deliberate about what we automate and what we preserve.
 
As technology leaders, we have five responsibilities:
 
1. Protect learning. 
Make sure people still build, debug and investigate, rather than just approve what the machine produces.
 
2. Preserve agency. 
Engineers must be able to explain and defend important technical decisions, even when they disagree with AI.
 
3. Design for augmentation. 
Use AI to expand what people can achieve, not just to reduce headcount.
 
4. Govern autonomy. 
Give AI systems authority step by step, with clear boundaries and escalation paths.
 
5. Cultivate curiosity. 
Reward people who ask better questions, not just those who produce answers quickly.
 
Hiring expertise gives us capability today. Developing people gives us the capacity to create capability tomorrow.
 
AI makes the first easier to get. It makes the second more important.
 
My question for every technology leadership team:
 
Are we using AI to make our people more capable, or are we slowly removing the experiences that make them capable in the first place?
 
The organisation that wins in the long run may not be the one with the most impressive technical talent today.
 
It may be the one that knows how to keep creating it.

posts.text:
starting my own business, I always had one simple question: How do companies hire people?

I would see some employees doing absolutely nothing while others seemed to carry the entire workload. It made me wonder how companies identify the right people and, more importantly, how they recognize those who genuinely bring value to the table.

When I started my own business, I faced that question firsthand. I had to decide whether to bring people on as employees or offer them shares in the company. I ultimately chose to build a team through hiring, and let me tell you, the recruitment and interview process was one of the longest and most interesting experiences!

I experimented with different hiring methods, but two qualities were particularly important to me: confidence and sharpness.

Long story short, I got incredibly lucky with an amazing team of UI/UX designers and IT engineers, both front-end and back-end.

There is one interview I will never forget. My final interview was with a front-end engineer, and I was genuinely indecisive. She was asking for a higher salary than the other candidates, and I wasn’t sure whether to meet her expectations.

Then she said something that stuck with me:

“I like working with you. I believe in your vision, and I promise you that if you hire me, you won’t regret it.”

At first, I thought it sounded a little bold, perhaps even cocky. But after thinking about it, I realized something: I liked her confidence. She reminded me of someone who knows exactly what value they bring to the table and isn’t afraid to communicate it.

I accepted her counteroffer, hired her, and it turned out to be one of the best hiring decisions I’ve ever made.

Today, that team feels like family. I couldn’t be happier to work alongside such talented, passionate, loving, and caring individuals.

It taught me something important: hiring isn’t just about finding someone who can do the job. It’s about finding people who believe in the vision, understand their value, and genuinely want to contribute to something bigger.

Now I’m curious:

What hiring methods have worked for you? What questions do you ask, what qualities do you look for, and what hiring decisions have surprised you the most?

I’d love to hear about your experiences, both the successes and the lessons learned.

#Entrepreneurship #Leadership #Hiring #Recruitment #TeamBuilding #StartupLife #BusinessGrowth #TalentAcquisition #CompanyCulture #LeadershipLess

The man who ran Meta's finances for eight years just left to join a four-year-old startup. The valuation explains why.

Dave Wehner confirmed on 7 November that he is leaving Meta, where he was chief strategy officer and chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022, to become CFO of Fireworks.

Fireworks was founded in 2022 by Lin Qiao, a Fudan computer science graduate who spent seven years at Facebook running PyTorch and AI compiler teams with more than 300 engineers.

The capital history is compressed. Fireworks raised at a USD 552 million valuation in July 2024, USD 4 billion in October 2025, and USD 17.5 billion in July 2026 on a USD 1.505 billion round. That is roughly 32 times in two years.

Revenue followed rather than trailed. Annualised revenue passed USD 280 million in October 2025 and USD 1 billion by July 2026, with more than 40 trillion tokens processed a day.

Hiring a CFO with public-company experience at a USD 17.5 billion private valuation reads as pre-IPO housekeeping. No listing has been announced.

The Chinese founder angle is not capital leaving China. It is where Chinese-trained engineers end up running the plumbing of American AI.

✔️  Bachelor's Degree in Computer Science, IT, Engineering, or a related field.

A Sincere Request to My LinkedIn Community: Seeking Guidance in Higher Education

I am reaching out with a sincere request—and, quite frankly, some frustration and disappointment.

I have spent 35 years in education, teaching elementary students, mentoring educators, developing curriculum, and sharing my knowledge with others. I earned my PhD in K–12 Studies in Education in 2019, hoping to one day extend my passion into higher education, particularly in a university's School of Education, preparing future teachers.

For approximately six years, I've had the privilege of serving as a Site Supervisor for Grand Canyon University, supporting teacher candidates entering the profession. I absolutely love this work! Helping aspiring teachers build confidence, knowledge, and classroom skills is incredibly rewarding. I am also a children's book author, curriculum developer, and literacy advocate.

Yet, since 2019, I have applied for numerous higher education positions, particularly adjunct faculty roles, and received rejection letter after rejection letter.

I have invested money in professional résumé and CV reviews, revised cover letters, and kept applying. Still, I ask myself: What am I missing?

My most recent rejection letter commended my “fine qualifications and professional accomplishments” before informing me that the institution was moving forward with other candidates. I know credentials and experience don't guarantee a position. But after years of applying, I would genuinely appreciate understanding why I am not advancing.

So, I am asking my LinkedIn community for help.

Is there someone in university human resources, academic recruitment, faculty hiring, or a School of Education who would be willing to volunteer a little of their time to review my CV, cover letter, or overall qualifications?

I am not asking anyone to offer me a job. I am asking for an honest, professional assessment and constructive guidance. What could I improve? Are there gaps in my qualifications? How might I better position my experience for university teaching?

I firmly believe God sometimes redirects our paths without removing the passion He placed within us. My professional journey has taken unexpected turns, but my desire to teach, mentor, and prepare future educators has never diminished.

After 35 years in the classroom, I still believe I have something valuable to contribute to the next generation of teachers.

Sometimes, all we need is someone willing to share their expertise and help us see what we may be overlooking.

If you can offer guidance, I would sincerely appreciate connecting with you. If you know someone who might help, please consider sharing this post.

Thank you for reading my story.

Settlement for Finch’s skill, agent and task markets is now live on Avalanche. On Finch, businesses hire AI agents, developers sell skills to the agents that need them, and companies post funded growth tasks for agents to complete. All of these transactions can now settle on Avalanche.

▸ 𝐌𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐡
Finch brings the AI agent economy onto one platform, built around four markets:
· 𝐀𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭: agents carry a portable identity and a verifiable work history. Businesses hire by track record
· 𝐒𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭: developers list reusable AI skills with clear ownership and earn on every sale and invocation
· 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭: industry experts turn their know-how into deployable AI workflows
· 𝐓𝐚𝐬𝐤 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭: funded tasks are escrowed and settle automatically once delivery is verified

Finch now serves 𝟑𝟔,𝟕𝟏𝟕 platform users.

▸ 𝐋𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐝𝐚𝐲
Buying and invoking skills, hiring agents, and escrowing and paying out tasks all settle on Avalanche. Post a task, have an agent with the right skills take it, verify delivery and settle, all without leaving the network.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐞: it brings payments, tokenization and global markets together on one network. That is the foundation autonomous agents need: fast settlement and assets that move freely across markets.

▸ 𝐍𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐄𝐑𝐂 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐬, 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐀𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩 𝐛𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩
The Finch team has authored nine ERC proposals that define the shared rules of the agent economy: skills and tasks as assets, agent identity and trust, collective decisions and swarms, resource discovery, economic valuation, and agent safety. All nine have Ethereum ERC numbers. ERC-8436 and ERC-8444 have been accepted into the official Ethereum ERC repository and are live on the EIP site in Draft status.

The first to deploy on Avalanche are ERC-8338 (Executable Skills) and ERC-8434 (Agent Identity). The rest will follow as they mature through Ethereum community review.

“The AI world needs an independent, efficient system of production and interaction of its own. The AI protocol standards we have initiated will provide the foundational framework, and the AIFi and AI Market we are building will mature on top of them.” (The Finch team)

▸ 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝
Today is a starting point. More agents, skills, funded tasks and AI-native assets are coming to Avalanche. The goal is to make Avalanche one of the main places where AI agents are hired, paid and valued.

posts.text:
Worldpay needed a new Asian payment route in three months. It took a chance on a 20-person startup that still had to build it.

That was InstaReM, now Nium, in 2016. A mentor had introduced the companies. Worldpay needed a provider to handle payouts to drivers and hosts in a new market. 

Worldpay’s Olann Kerrison later recalled evaluating several providers. 

InstaReM’s developers built a functioning back office in about 24 hours, helping convince him they could deliver.

They went live that October. Founder Prajit Nanu says the first month brought 100,000 payouts. 

The country requirement arrived with an enterprise buyer, a specific job and a deadline.

For the next APAC expansion, revisit opportunities stalled because you couldn’t serve a particular country.

A buyer asking whether you cover Malaysia is a clue. 

A buyer naming the project, launch date and condition for appointing you gives Sales something concrete to test.

Take that requirement to similar companies in the same country and industry. 

Track who progresses towards an evaluation or proposal, not who agrees the problem sounds interesting.

If nobody else progresses, assess the first deal on whether it can pay for the capability you need to build. Don’t automatically attach an office and a local hiring plan.

A large customer can justify entering a market without proving there’s a market beyond that customer.

posts.text:
30 Days Beyond the Job Search: Week 1

Eight days in, and I've already had some experiences I definitely wouldn't have had otherwise. I'm really glad I decided to give this a shot.

Here's what I've been up to since kicking things off with Be Kind last Sunday:

Day 2: Learn something new. Attended the first annual AI for Small Business Conference with the New Jersey Small Business Development Center (NJSBDC) in Mercer County. Interesting to hear how small businesses are thinking about AI, and a great opportunity to meet people outside my usual circles. 

Day 3: Check on a job seeker. Caught up with Shruthi Puppala and talked through her job search. She's a super talented developer with strong database and excellent client-facing skills who's also looking for her next opportunity. If you're hiring someone with that combination, she's worth talking to!

Day 4: Finish a postponed project. Finally tackled a storage closet I'd been avoiding for far too long. What I thought would be a quick cleanup turned into a much bigger project than expected. Definitely a sense of accomplishment at the end of that one.

Day 5: Thank a mentor. Sent a note to Dr. STEPHEN SUN, who's had a big impact on me and my career and has been a great source of support. It's easy to appreciate someone without ever taking the time to tell them. I'm glad I finally did.

Day 6: Reconnect with an old friend. Had a really fun lunch with Don Golder, a terrific corporate controller who's also looking for his next role. And he has a great sense of humor, which isn't necessarily what you expect from someone who works with spreadsheets all day! It had been entirely too long since I'd seen him.

Day 7: Try something new. This one really took me out of my comfort zone. I set up a sign on Princeton's campus offering free portraits to strangers. For a while, nobody stopped. So I put the sign away and started approaching people myself. The first person said yes, and then came families, students, and some wonderful conversations. I connected with a couple of professional photographers, someone insisted on giving me a generous tip despite the pictures being free, and I ended up sending some beautiful portraits and got messages back telling me I'd made their day. I was nervous going in, but I'd absolutely do it again.

Day 8: Take a mindful walk. Today I slowed things down and left my phone behind. I tried to pay attention to what I could see, hear, smell, and feel. My mind wandered to the past and future, but whenever I noticed, I brought myself back. I watched leaves fall from the trees and sail down a stream, spotted a snake, and had a tired dragonfly land on my hand. A peaceful, grounding way to end the week (and prepare for another busy week ahead).

Seven very different experiences, and I got something out of every one of them. The biggest surprise so far is how much I've enjoyed doing things I might otherwise have put off or never tried at all.

22 days to go!

posts.text:
How to go from Senior Engineer to Technical Lead: 6 things I'd focus on.
I went from junior developer (2020) to Technical Lead (2026). Nobody handed me a map, so here's the one I wish I'd had.
1. Own an outcome, not just a task.
Don't stop at "my ticket is done." Ask whether the feature actually works for the people using it. Leads are trusted with results.
2. Learn to explain trade-offs.
"We chose A over B because of cost, time, and risk" is a lead's sentence. "A is better" is not.
3. Write things down.
Design notes, decision records, short runbooks. Writing scales your thinking beyond the meeting you were in.
4. Review code to teach, not to judge.
One kind, clear comment that explains why helps a teammate more than ten corrections.
5. Raise problems early, with a proposal.
"Here's the risk, and here's what I suggest" builds trust faster than either silence or complaining.
6. Make the people around you better.
Pair with juniors. Share what you learn. A lead's growth is measured by the team's growth.
You don't need the title to start. Do these in your current role, and the title usually follows.
Which of these are you working on right now? Tell me below 👇
I'm open to my next role as a Technical Lead, Senior .NET Engineer, or Architect. If your team is hiring, my DMs are open.

posts.text:
What happens when companies need experienced workers but stop hiring beginners?

I have been thinking about this question while reading research from Stanford.

In an August 2026 update, researchers examining US payroll data found that employment among 22–25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations was approximately 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with their less-exposed peers.

Interestingly, the difference appeared primarily through reduced hiring, rather than increased layoffs.

The researchers caution that this does not establish AI as the cause.

But the finding raises a question that goes beyond today's employment numbers.

Consider how people become experienced professionals.

A junior software developer learns by writing code, fixing defects, and understanding why systems fail. A young analyst develops judgment by examining data, making mistakes, and learning from feedback.

These activities are not merely tasks to be completed. They are also how professional expertise develops.

If organisations increasingly automate such work, they may improve immediate productivity while unintentionally reducing opportunities for beginners to gain experience.

That creates a possible long-term problem.

Companies may eventually need experienced professionals without having invested enough in developing them.

Perhaps the next important question about AI and employment is not simply how many jobs technology can replace.

It is who will develop tomorrow's experienced workers if fewer people are given the opportunity to begin.

Source: Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 12 August 2026.

posts.text:
🧱 From Boxes to Building Blocks 🧱

I've worked in software engineering, program management, business development, consulting, and IT recruitment. Looking back, tech was easier to sort into boxes. 📦 Software, hardware, and infrastructure mostly sat in the customer's own data center. It wasn't easy, but it was clear who owned what.

Then things shifted. Microsoft's "Software Plus Services" push, and later hybrid cloud, let companies keep some things in house and hand others to outside providers. What I first saw as fragmentation, I now see as specialization. 


🔍 Specialization Is Showing Up Everywhere 🔍

We build differently now, too. Tools like React help developers organize big, complex apps. Splitting applications into services creates clearer boundaries, though the complexity just moves into the connections between the pieces. 


🎓 Certifications Got More Specific 🎓

Certifications followed the same path. Labels like Java, Oracle, and PeopleSoft once covered a lot of ground. Today, Microsoft has moved from MCSA, MCSD, and MCSE to role based certifications, and Kubernetes has separate credentials for administration, development, and security. Expertise is now described in smaller, more precise pieces. 


💡 Why Certifications Still Matter Now 💡

When job requirements get specific, employers want clearer evidence of what someone knows. In the Linux Foundation's 2025 State of Tech Talent survey, 71% of organizations said certifications are important when evaluating technical skills. Hands on experience and portfolios ranked even higher, so think of a certification as a solid starting point, not the whole story. 


🤝 A Win for Recruiters 🤝

From my recruiting days, I can tell you this helps recruiters, too. "Cloud engineer" only tells you so much. A relevant certification helps a recruiter ask sharper screening questions, compare candidates to what the hiring manager needs, and spot where more assessment is needed. Just know what each credential covers, since a foundational cert and an implementation focused cert aren't the same. It's about matching evidence to the work, not counting badges. 


🏁 Make Your Skills Easy to Recognize 🏁

A certification won't erase onboarding, since knowing a platform isn't the same as knowing a company's systems and team habits. Even AWS says there's "no true substitute for experience." Still, a relevant cert plus recent project work can shorten the road to contributing. 🚀 

In a tough job market, pick certifications that fit the work you want, pair them with real examples of what you've built or improved, and share that story with confidence. 🙌 

Certifications give employers a clearer starting point and a credible case that you can do the work. ✨

Happy Monday!  I keep reading that the collapse of Bathla “sent shockwaves through the Australian CRE private credit market”.  Also, there seems to be a broad assumption that those invested, will all miss out on their returns.

I think these assumptions and commentary misses an important distinction.  A developer collapse is a serious event, but it doesn’t, on its own, tell us the eventual outcome for each lender or its investors.  That depends on the individual exposure, the security held, the remaining costs and the options available to recover capital.

Strong, proactive asset management and access to construction and development expertise can make a significant difference.  Many funds use moment like this to develop opportunities, even if its hard work to get there.

Two research notes I read over the weekend  😎 raise a related question: does the team have the experience needed for the existing loan book, as well as the next transaction? And can they explain it clearly when raising capital?

Debtwire reported Australian private credit deal volumes fell from $12.6bn in Q4 2025 to $2.4bn in Q3 2026. Real estate accounted for about 40% of reported deal volume across the first nine months of this year.

Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer separately describes the market as entering its first meaningful workout cycle, with greater emphasis on portfolio management, refinancing risk and valuations.

Neither finding means new lending stops. But managing existing exposures and assessing new opportunities require different capabilities.

“Credit experience” can mean originating and underwriting a loan. It can also mean monitoring covenants, negotiating an extension, assessing an enforcement option or managing a restructuring. Those aren’t interchangeable experiences.

Capital raising, investor relations and investor reporting teams also need to understand what has changed, what remains uncertain and what investors need to know.

For job seekers, describe the decisions and outcomes you were responsible for, not just the size of the book. For hiring managers, be clear about which capabilities you need to add and which your team already has.

Feel free to reach out if any questions on this subject.

posts.text:
Most plans to hire a software team in Manila start in a spreadsheet. Average developer salary, times three, done.

Six months later one role is still open, the first hire is waiting on architecture decisions nobody in the company can make, and operations still run on the sheets the project was meant to replace.

Salary is the part of the cost people see. The spreadsheet usually leaves out the rest:

13th-month pay and statutory contributions.
HMO with dependents, which senior people expect.
Recruiting fees, or weeks of your own leadership screening CVs.
Notice periods, then the months before new hires work as a team.
The engineer who leaves in month nine and takes the context with them.

And the cost nobody budgets for: who reviews the code? A COO can tell when a finance controller is struggling. Nobody can tell from a Friday demo that the code underneath is quietly breaking.

Hiring in-house is the right call once you have a CTO whose job is recruiting and reviewing engineers. Before that, you are paying for headcount, not capacity.

I wrote up the full comparison: in-house, freelancers, staff augmentation and an embedded senior team. Link in the comments.

posts.text:
The IT job market isn't broken. It's stuck in a search problem, and economists won a Nobel Prize for explaining it.
⠀
Developers send hundreds of applications and hear nothing back. Companies get floods of resumes and still say they can't find good people. Both are true at once.
⠀
In 2010, Diamond, Mortensen and Pissarides won the Nobel Prize in Economics for search-and-matching theory. In their model, hiring isn't a simple count of jobs against candidates. Finding the right match takes time and costs money on both sides, so open vacancies and unemployment can exist side by side.
⠀
What surprised me most: suppose people find jobs half as fast as before. Unemployment can nearly double, even if no one else is laid off.
⠀
AI has made this worse, at least for now. Applying is almost free, so candidates mass-apply. Employers answer with automated screening. We now have information that is cheap to produce and expensive to verify.
⠀
Pissarides doesn't expect AI to wipe out jobs on a mass scale. His bigger worry is the bottom rung. If AI takes over junior work, where will tomorrow's senior specialists come from?
⠀
So "cheap to generate, expensive to verify" isn't only a hiring problem. It's the central question for any system that runs on AI.
⠀
How are you separating real signal from AI-generated noise in hiring right now?

posts.text:
Every missed call is a patient who books with the next clinic. 📞 
So I built an AI receptionist for dental clinics, and it’s live. 😍 

It answers the phone in a natural voice, checks opening hours, and takes the booking request. The clinic’s staff then see the full transcript and a call summary in a private dashboard.
In the demo call, the caller asks for 12 AM. The assistant says the clinic is closed and offers 12 PM instead. The booking request lands on the schedule.
What’s under the hood:

→ Voice layer: Vapi (the call, speech and turn-taking)
→ Backend: Fastify + TypeScript, inputs validated with zod, webhook protected by a shared secret
→ Booking logic: opening hours, visit lengths and lead time in tested functions; Postgres advisory lock so two callers can’t take the same slot
→ Dashboard: Next.js 15 + React 19, signed-cookie login
→ Public demo reads a masked feed only: no phone numbers, no transcripts.

The clinic is fictional, but the build is real and you can try it yourself.
I’m a Senior Full Stack Engineer (React, Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, Python, Postgres, AWS) with 5+ years of experience. I’m open to remote contract roles, and I build AI assistants and web apps for small businesses.

If you’re hiring, or you run a clinic or service business that loses calls, send me a message.

Role: Full-Stack Next.js / TypeScript Engineer (SaaS & AI Infrastructure)
Location: Remote (India)
Type: Full-time / Long-term Contract
Email: hr@avantisofttech.com

About the Role
We are looking for an experienced Full-Stack Next.js / TypeScript Engineer to own technical maintenance, production reliability, and feature evolution for Statemento, a high-performance financial AI platform that converts complex bank statements into structured spreadsheets (Excel, CSV, QuickBooks).

Our entire stack is built in a modern, unified TypeScript ecosystem—no context-switching between backend languages. You will work directly on serverless architecture, AI extraction pipelines, database integrity, and webhook-driven billing systems.

What You’ll Do
Maintain & Scale the Core App: Own full-stack development across our Next.js App Router, React Server/Client Components, and Node.js serverless runtimes.

Refine AI Extraction Pipelines: Maintain and optimize document parsing workflows using LLM APIs (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI) and local PDF text processors (unpdf), ensuring strict balance reconciliation and zero data leakage.

Database & Auth Operations: Manage PostgreSQL on Supabase, write and deploy schema migrations, enforce strict Row-Level Security (RLS) policies, and debug connection pooling.

Payment & Subscription Lifecycle: Maintain our Merchant of Record integrations (Lemon Squeezy), including webhook event listeners, signature validation, idempotency guards, and customer entitlement syncs.

Production Reliability & Bug Triage: Monitor application health across Vercel, Supabase, and Upstash Redis. Diagnose and resolve edge-case PDF conversion issues and balance check discrepancies.

Testing & Code Quality: Run and expand automated test suites using TypeScript and Node’s native test runner (tsx).

What We’re Looking For
3–6 years of professional software engineering experience, with substantial production experience in TypeScript and modern Next.js (App Router).

Strong Database Fundamentals: Hands-on experience with PostgreSQL, schema design, and Supabase (specifically writing secure RLS policies).

Serverless & Webhook Proficiency: Solid understanding of stateless API design, HMAC signature verification, idempotency patterns, and asynchronous error boundaries.

Low-Level Data Handling: Comfortable working with Node.js streams, buffers (Uint8Array), and file transformations (CSV, XLSX).

Autonomous Problem Solver: High ownership mindset

Our Tech Stack
Frontend & Backend: Next.js (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
Data & Storage: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Upstash Redis (rate limiting)
Hosting & Runtime: Vercel Edge/Serverless, Node.js 24
AI & Document Processing: Anthropic Claude API, OpenAI API, unpdf, write-excel-file


How to Apply
Send your resume and a link to your GitHub profile (or portfolio) to [Insert Contact Email / Link].

posts.text:
New here, or been reading all week? One post about working with me — then back to the useful stuff.

I am Muhammad Hamad, a Full Stack Developer and AI Engineer with 8 years of experience, working remotely with clients and teams worldwide.

Most good projects I have seen do not start with "build us an AI system". They start with one workflow that wastes a team's week.

So here is how working with me usually starts:

1. You describe the workflow that wastes your team's time — leads, data entry, follow-ups, documents, support.
2. I tell you honestly whether AI, automation, or simple software is the right fix — including when the answer is "do not build anything yet".
3. We start narrow: one task, clear rules, a human checking the important steps. Then we expand only if it works.

What I build around that first step: workflow automation, AI features and agents with rules and limits you control, and the software around them — SaaS platforms, dashboards, and internal tools.

My stack: Python, TypeScript, React, Next.js, NestJS, FastAPI — plus OpenAI and Claude APIs, LangChain, and retrieval systems.

Two ways to start a conversation:
- Businesses: message me the workflow. I will reply with the first step I would take.
- Recruiters and hiring managers: message me the role. My portfolio and experience are at hamadshafiq.com.

No pressure, no pitch beyond this post. Tomorrow we go back to teaching.

Which workflow would you bring to that first conversation?

#Automation #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAgents #BusinessAutomation #Workflow #SoftwareDevelopment #SaaS #FullStackDeveloper #AI #FutureOfWork

🚀 We’re Hiring: Technology Intern (Remote)

Heroic Apparel is growing, and we’re looking for a curious, hands-on Technology Intern to help build and run the digital side of our brand. You’ll work on our website, online store and internal tools.

📍 Location: Remote (India)
 💼 Experience: 0–1 year (freshers welcome)
 ⏳ Duration: 6 months

 🕒 Type: Internship

What you’ll work on

Build and maintain features across our web stack, front end and back end
Manage and customise our WordPress / WooCommerce site: themes, plugins, speed and SEO basics
Deploy and monitor services on AWS (EC2, S3, Lightsail, CloudFront, Route 53)
Connect our store with payment gateways, shipping partners and inventory tools through APIs
Automate everyday tasks such as order updates, product uploads and reports
Fix bugs, improve site speed and keep security up to date
Work with the design and marketing teams on landing pages and sale campaigns

What we’re looking for

Good grasp of HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Familiarity with at least one stack: MERN, PHP/Laravel, Python/Django, or similar
Working knowledge of WordPress (WooCommerce is a big plus)
Basic understanding of AWS or another cloud platform
Comfort with Git/GitHub and REST APIs
Basic SQL or MongoDB
Problem-solving mindset and willingness to learn quickly
Clear communication and ownership when working remotely

Good to have

Experience with Shopify, headless commerce, or Next.js/React
Exposure to Docker, CI/CD, or serverless (AWS Lambda)
Knowledge of SEO, Google Analytics or Meta Pixel
Interest in fashion, D2C brands or e-commerce
A portfolio, GitHub profile or live project we can see

What you’ll get

 ✅ Real ownership of a live e-commerce brand’s tech
 ✅ Mentorship and hands-on learning across the full stack and cloud
 ✅ Flexible remote work and hours
 ✅ Internship certificate and Letter of Recommendation
 ✅ Exclusive Heroic Apparel merch 👕

How to apply
Send your resume, GitHub or portfolio link, and a few lines on a project you’re proud of to hire@heroicapparel.in
Subject line: Technology Intern – [Your Name]

Heroic Apparel is an equal-opportunity employer. We welcome applicants from all backgrounds.
